  namespace: shop
roleRef: { kind: Role, name: pod-reader, apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io }
# Check permissions
# kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n shop --as system:serviceaccount:shop:ci-bot
# kubectl auth can-i --list -n shop
keyPoints: Principle of least privilege: avoid cluster-admin; grant verbs on specific resources
Set automountServiceAccountToken: false for Pods that never call the API
Cloud workload identity (IRSA on EKS, Workload Identity on GKE) maps a ServiceAccount to cloud IAM without static keys
Audit who can read Secrets and exec into Pods — those are effectively admin rights

concepts.name: Pod Security & Hardening
concepts.explanation: Pods should run with the least privilege possible. Pod Security Admission (the replacement for removed PodSecurityPolicy) enforces the Baseline and Restricted standards per namespace, and securityContext settings harden each container.
concepts.code:
# Enforce the "restricted" standard on a namespace
kubectl label ns shop pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted

# Hardened container
# spec:
#   securityContext:
#     runAsNonRoot: true
#     runAsUser: 10001
#     seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }
#   containers:
#   - name: app
#     securityContext:
#       allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
#       readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
#       capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
#
# Other layers: NetworkPolicy, image scanning/signing, admission policies
#   (Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy), runtime detection (Falco),
#   encrypted etcd, private API endpoint, regular node patching
keyPoints: privileged: true or hostPath mounts effectively give root on the node — avoid them
readOnlyRootFilesystem needs writable emptyDir mounts for temp directories
Use admission policies to enforce rules (no :latest, require limits, trusted registries)
CIS Kubernetes Benchmark and tools like kube-bench and kubescape check your cluster configuration

concepts.name: Debugging Workflow for Any Broken Pod
concepts.explanation: Debug from the outside in: status, events, logs, then inside the container. This simple order resolves most issues quickly and is exactly how to answer "a pod is not working, what do you do?" in an interview.
concepts.code:
kubectl get pods -o wide                       # 1. status, restarts, node
kubectl describe pod <pod>                     # 2. Events: scheduling, image, probe, OOM
kubectl logs <pod> [-c container] [--previous] # 3. app logs (previous = before crash)
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp    # 4. cluster-wide clues
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh                   # 5. look inside (env, DNS, connectivity)
kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=<container>   # ephemeral debug container
kubectl debug node/<node> -it --image=busybox  # shell on a node
kubectl get endpoints <svc>                    # is the Service selecting Pods?
kubectl port-forward <pod> 8080:8080           # test directly, bypassing Service/Ingress
kubectl top pod <pod>                          # resource pressure
kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml | less           # the real, full spec and status
keyPoints: Read the Events section of kubectl describe first — it often states the cause plainly
Use ephemeral debug containers for distroless images that have no shell
Always compare the Service selector with Pod labels when traffic does not arrive
Check one layer at a time: Pod → Service → Ingress/Gateway → DNS → external LB

concepts.name: Common Pod Failure States & Fixes
concepts.explanation: Each Pod status points to a specific category of problem. Memorising this table is high-value for both real incidents and interviews.
concepts.code:
# STATUS               MEANING / USUAL CAUSE                          FIX
# Pending              no node fits: not enough CPU/mem, taints,      describe pod -> "FailedScheduling";
#                      unbound PVC, nodeSelector mismatch             add nodes, fix requests/affinity/PVC
# ContainerCreating    pulling image, mounting volume, CNI issue      describe pod events
# ImagePullBackOff /   wrong image name/tag, private registry         fix image; create imagePullSecret;
#  ErrImagePull        without credentials, rate limit                check registry auth
# CrashLoopBackOff     app starts then exits repeatedly               kubectl logs --previous; check
#                      (bad config, missing env, bug, failing probe)  command, config, dependencies
# OOMKilled (137)      exceeded memory limit                          raise limit or fix leak
# Error / Completed    one-off container exited                       check exit code and logs
# Terminating (stuck)  finalizer or node down                         kubectl delete pod --force --grace-period=0
# Evicted              node under disk/memory pressure                free node resources, set requests
# Running but 0/1      readiness probe failing                        check probe path/port, app logs
kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[*].lastState}'
kubectl describe node <node> | grep -A5 Conditions
keyPoints: CrashLoopBackOff is a symptom, not a cause — the answer is always in the previous logs
Exit code 137 = SIGKILL (often OOM); 143 = SIGTERM; 1 = application error
Pending with "Insufficient cpu" means requests are too large or the cluster is full
Force-deleting Pods can orphan resources; remove finalizers carefully

concepts.name: Debugging Services, DNS & Networking
concepts.explanation: When Pods run but nothing connects, isolate the network layer. Check that the Service has endpoints, DNS resolves, and no NetworkPolicy blocks the path. A throwaway debug Pod with networking tools is the fastest way to test from inside the cluster.
concepts.code:
kubectl get svc,endpoints web
kubectl describe svc web                      # Selector, Port, TargetPort, Endpoints
kubectl run net --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash
#   inside: nslookup web.default.svc.cluster.local
#           curl -v http://web:80/ ;   nc -zv db 5432
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns         # CoreDNS logs
kubectl get netpol -A                                     # anything blocking?
kubectl get ingress,gateway,httproute -A
kubectl logs -n <ingress-ns> deploy/<ingress-controller>
# Typical findings
#  - Endpoints empty              -> selector/label mismatch or readiness failing
#  - targetPort != containerPort  -> connection refused
#  - NodePort/LB unreachable      -> cloud security group or firewall
#  - DNS timeouts                 -> CoreDNS overloaded, ndots/search-domain issues
keyPoints: Test in layers: Pod IP, then Service ClusterIP, then DNS name, then Ingress
The ndots:5 default can cause extra DNS lookups; use fully qualified names for external hosts
502/503 from an Ingress usually means no healthy endpoints behind the backend Service
504 means the backend was too slow — check timeouts and Pod resource saturation

concepts.name: Helm: The Kubernetes Package Manager
concepts.explanation: Helm packages Kubernetes manifests into a chart: templates plus default values. You install a chart as a release and override settings per environment with values files. Helm is how most third-party software (Prometheus, ingress controllers, cert-manager) is installed. Helm 4 is current; note --atomic is now --rollback-on-failure and --force is --force-replace.
concepts.code:
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo update
helm search repo nginx
helm show values bitnami/nginx > values.yaml        # see every option

helm install web bitnami/nginx -n shop --create-namespace -f values-prod.yaml --set replicaCount=3
helm upgrade --install web ./charts/web -n shop -f values-prod.yaml \
  --set image.tag=1.4.2 --rollback-on-failure --wait --timeout 5m     # Helm 4 (Helm 3: --atomic)
helm list -A; helm status web -n shop
helm get values web -n shop; helm get manifest web -n shop
helm history web -n shop
helm rollback web 2 -n shop
helm uninstall web -n shop

helm template web ./charts/web -f values-prod.yaml   # render locally, no cluster
helm lint ./charts/web
helm diff upgrade web ./charts/web -f values-prod.yaml   # plugin: preview changes
helm package ./charts/web; helm push web-1.0.0.tgz oci://ghcr.io/myorg/charts
keyPoints: upgrade --install is idempotent — the standard command for CI/CD
Always review rendered output with helm template or helm diff before production upgrades
Charts can be stored in OCI registries (ECR, GHCR) just like images
Helm 4 uses server-side apply for new releases and needs the watch permission for --wait

concepts.name: Anatomy of a Helm Chart & Templating
concepts.explanation: A chart is a folder with a fixed layout. Templates use Go templating with values from values.yaml, so one chart serves every environment. Helper templates (_helpers.tpl) avoid repeating names and labels.
concepts.code:
# mychart/
#   Chart.yaml          name, version (chart), appVersion (your app)
#   values.yaml         defaults
#   templates/
#     deployment.yaml
#     service.yaml
#     ingress.yaml
#     _helpers.tpl      named templates, not rendered directly
#     NOTES.txt         message after install
#   charts/             sub-chart dependencies
#
# templates/deployment.yaml (fragment)
# apiVersion: apps/v1
# kind: Deployment
# metadata:
#   name: {{ include "mychart.fullname" . }}
# spec:
#   replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
#   template:
#     metadata:
#       annotations:
#         checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}
#     spec:
#       containers:
#       - name: app
#         image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag | default .Chart.AppVersion }}"
#         {{- with .Values.resources }}
#         resources: {{- toYaml . | nindent 12 }}
#         {{- end }}
#         {{- if .Values.ingress.enabled }} ... {{- end }}
helm create mychart
helm dependency update ./mychart
keyPoints: Use toYaml | nindent N to inject blocks with correct indentation
The checksum annotation restarts Pods automatically when a ConfigMap changes
Chart version changes when the chart changes; appVersion tracks the application version
Keep values.yaml documented and minimal — fewer knobs mean fewer bugs

concepts.name: Kustomize: Overlays Without Templates
concepts.explanation: Kustomize customises plain YAML by layering patches, so there is no templating language. A base holds the common manifests and each overlay (dev, staging, prod) patches only what differs. It is built into kubectl.
concepts.code:
# k8s/
#   base/            deployment.yaml service.yaml kustomization.yaml
#   overlays/dev/    kustomization.yaml
#   overlays/prod/   kustomization.yaml patch-replicas.yaml
#
# overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
# apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
# kind: Kustomization
# resources: [../../base]
# namespace: shop-prod
# namePrefix: prod-
# images:
# - { name: myorg/web, newTag: 1.4.2 }
# patches:
# - path: patch-replicas.yaml
# configMapGenerator:
# - name: app-config
#   literals: [LOG_LEVEL=warn]
kubectl kustomize overlays/prod            # render
kubectl apply -k overlays/prod             # apply
kustomize edit set image myorg/web=myorg/web:1.4.3    # CI-friendly image bump
keyPoints: Helm for packaging and distributing; Kustomize for environment differences — they are often combined
configMapGenerator appends a content hash so a config change triggers a rollout
ArgoCD and Flux both understand Kustomize natively
Prefer small, focused patches over copying whole files into overlays

concepts.name: CI, Continuous Delivery & Continuous Deployment
concepts.explanation: Continuous Integration means developers merge small changes into the main branch frequently, and every merge is automatically built and tested. Continuous Delivery keeps the main branch always releasable, with a manual approval to ship. Continuous Deployment removes that approval so every change that passes the pipeline goes to production automatically.
concepts.code:
# CI (Continuous Integration)
#   commit -> build -> unit tests -> lint -> security scan -> artifact
#   Goal: find integration problems within minutes, not weeks
#
# CD (Continuous Delivery)
#   CI + auto-deploy to staging + automated tests + [manual approval] -> prod
#
# CD (Continuous Deployment)
#   CI + auto-deploy to staging + tests -> prod automatically (no human gate)
#
# Pipeline = a sequence of stages; each stage = jobs; each job = steps (commands)
#   Fast feedback first (lint, unit) -> slower checks later (integration, e2e)
keyPoints: The abbreviation CD is ambiguous — always say which one you mean in interviews
A broken main branch is the team's top priority; fix or revert immediately
Pipelines must be fast: aim for under 10 minutes for the PR feedback loop
Pipeline definitions live in the repo (pipeline as code), reviewed like application code

concepts.name: Anatomy of a Good Pipeline
concepts.explanation: A good pipeline fails fast, builds once, and promotes the same artifact through environments. Each stage adds more confidence, and every step is repeatable and logged. Treat the pipeline as a product: monitor its duration and flakiness.
concepts.code:
# 1. Checkout          get the exact commit
# 2. Lint / format     eslint, checkstyle, hadolint, terraform fmt, shellcheck
# 3. Build             compile, package, resolve dependencies (cached)
# 4. Unit tests        fast, parallel, with coverage report
# 5. Static analysis   SonarQube / Semgrep (SAST), dependency scan (SCA)
# 6. Package           docker build -> tag with git SHA -> push to registry
# 7. Image scan        trivy / grype; fail on HIGH+CRITICAL
# 8. Deploy to dev     automatic, via Helm/ArgoCD/Terraform
# 9. Integration/E2E   API tests, Playwright/Cypress, smoke tests
# 10. Deploy to staging -> load/perf test -> approval
# 11. Deploy to prod   canary/rolling + automatic verification + rollback on failure
# 12. Notify           Slack/Teams, update ticket, record deployment (DORA)
keyPoints: Run independent jobs in parallel (lint, unit test, scan) to cut wall-clock time
Cache dependencies and Docker layers; start from clean runners for reproducibility
Flaky tests destroy trust in the pipeline — quarantine and fix them fast
Run the same scripts locally and in CI (Makefile or task runner) so debugging is easy

concepts.name: Test Pyramid & Quality Gates
concepts.explanation: Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and very few slow end-to-end tests form the test pyramid. Quality gates are automatic pass/fail rules in the pipeline (coverage, vulnerabilities, code smells) that block a bad change before it merges.
concepts.code:
#          /\        E2E / UI tests   (few, slow, expensive)
#         /  \       Integration / API / contract tests (some)
#        /____\      Unit tests       (many, milliseconds)
#
# Other test types
#   Smoke      after deploy: is the app basically alive?
#   Regression re-check old behaviour
#   Load/perf  k6, JMeter, Gatling, Locust
#   Security   SAST, DAST (OWASP ZAP), dependency scan
#   Chaos      deliberately break things to prove resilience
#
# Example quality gates
#   - all tests pass            - coverage on new code >= 80%
#   - no HIGH/CRITICAL CVEs     - SonarQube quality gate = passed
#   - PR approved by 1+ reviewer - signed commits / required checks
keyPoints: Use testcontainers or compose to run real databases in integration tests
Contract tests (Pact) let microservices deploy independently with confidence
Shift-left: the earlier a bug is found, the cheaper it is to fix
Gates should be few and meaningful; too many slows delivery and invites bypassing

concepts.name: Artifacts, Registries & Package Management
concepts.explanation: A pipeline produces artifacts — container images, JARs, npm packages, Helm charts, binaries. Store them in a versioned registry, make them immutable, and deploy exactly those artifacts. Never rebuild for production.
concepts.code:
# Artifact type         Where it lives
# Container image       Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR, GCR/Artifact Registry, ACR, Harbor
# Java (JAR)            Maven Central, Nexus, Artifactory, GitHub Packages
# npm / Python / NuGet  npm registry, PyPI, private Nexus/Artifactory/CodeArtifact
# Helm chart            OCI registry (same registries as images)
# Terraform module      registry.terraform.io, private registry, Git tags
#
# Good practices
#   - immutable, versioned (semver + git SHA); never overwrite a published version
#   - retention/lifecycle policy to control storage cost
#   - vulnerability scan + signature + SBOM attached to each artifact
#   - dependency proxy/cache to survive upstream outages and rate limits
mvn deploy -DskipTests          # publish JAR to the configured repository
npm publish --provenance --access public
twine upload dist/*
keyPoints: Pin and lock dependencies (package-lock.json, poetry.lock, go.sum) for repeatable builds
Use a private proxy registry (Nexus, Artifactory, CodeArtifact) to guard against supply-chain attacks
Prefer short-lived OIDC credentials over long-lived tokens for publishing
Keep release notes and changelog generation automated

concepts.name: Deployment Strategies: Rolling, Blue/Green, Canary
concepts.explanation: A deployment strategy trades off speed, cost, risk and rollback time. Rolling replaces instances gradually; blue/green keeps two full environments and switches traffic; canary sends a small percentage of traffic to the new version first. Pick based on risk tolerance and infrastructure.
concepts.code:
# RECREATE     stop v1 -> start v2.  Simple, has downtime.
# ROLLING      replace instances in batches.  No downtime, both versions live briefly.
#              (Kubernetes default)  Rollback = roll forward/back again, takes time.
# BLUE/GREEN   deploy v2 beside v1 (green); test; flip the load balancer.
#              Instant rollback (flip back), but double the infrastructure cost.
# CANARY       route 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% of traffic to v2 while watching metrics.
#              Lowest blast radius; needs good metrics + traffic splitting
#              (Argo Rollouts, Flagger, Istio, Gateway API weights, ALB weighted targets).
# SHADOW       copy real traffic to v2, discard its responses (safe testing).
# A/B TEST     route by user segment to compare business metrics (a product decision).
#
# Decouple deploy from release with FEATURE FLAGS (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagsmith):
#   ship code dark, then enable for 1% -> 100% of users, kill-switch if it misbehaves.
keyPoints: Database changes must be backward compatible so old and new versions can run together
Automate the canary decision: promote or roll back from metrics (error rate, latency)
Blue/green is great for risky releases; canary is great for large user bases
Feature flags give the fastest rollback of all — flip a switch, no deploy

concepts.name: Database Migrations in Pipelines (Expand & Contract)
concepts.explanation: Application code can roll back instantly but a database schema cannot. The safe approach is expand and contract: make changes in small backward-compatible steps across several releases so that old and new application versions work with the same schema.
concepts.code:
# Example: rename column  users.name -> users.full_name
# Release 1 (expand)   ADD COLUMN full_name; app writes BOTH columns; backfill old rows
# Release 2 (migrate)  app reads full_name only
# Release 3 (contract) DROP COLUMN name       (only after Release 2 is stable)
#
# Rules
#  - never drop/rename in the same release that stops using the old column
#  - additive changes first (new nullable column, new table)
#  - large backfills in batches, off-peak, outside the deploy path
#  - every migration is versioned, in Git, applied by a tool, and idempotent
flyway -url=jdbc:postgresql://db/app -user=app migrate        # Flyway
liquibase update --changelog-file=db/changelog.xml            # Liquibase
alembic upgrade head                                          # Python/SQLAlchemy
npx prisma migrate deploy                                     # Prisma
keyPoints: Run migrations as a separate pipeline step or Kubernetes Job/initContainer, not in app startup on every replica
Test migrations on a copy of production-sized data before release
Take a backup or snapshot before destructive changes
"Roll forward" with a fix is often safer than rolling the database back

concepts.name: Workflow Syntax & Triggers
concepts.explanation: A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows/. It starts on events (triggers), runs one or more jobs on runners, and each job runs steps — either shell commands (run) or reusable actions (uses). Jobs run in parallel by default; use needs to order them.
concepts.code:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:                     # manual "Run workflow" button
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 3 * * 1"                  # weekly, UTC
permissions:
  contents: read                         # least privilege for GITHUB_TOKEN
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true               # cancel superseded runs
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test -- --coverage
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with: { name: coverage, path: coverage/ }
keyPoints: Triggers include push, pull_request, workflow_dispatch, schedule, release, workflow_call, and more
Set permissions explicitly; the default token can be broader than needed
Pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA for supply-chain safety (Dependabot can update them)
Action major versions move over time (checkout is at v7, setup-node v7) — check the marketplace for current versions

concepts.name: Matrix Builds, Caching, Artifacts & Outputs
concepts.explanation: Matrices run the same job across several versions or operating systems in parallel. Caching speeds up dependency installs, artifacts pass files between jobs, and outputs pass small values between steps and jobs.
concepts.code:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
        node: [22, 24]
        include:
          - os: ubuntu-latest
            node: 24
            experimental: true
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with: { node-version: "${{ matrix.node }}", cache: npm }
      - id: version
        run: echo "tag=$(git describe --tags --always)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"     # step output
      - run: echo "Building ${{ steps.version.outputs.tag }}"
      - uses: actions/cache@v6                  # generic cache
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/pip
          key: pip-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('**/requirements.txt') }}
          restore-keys: pip-${{ runner.os }}-
  deploy:
    needs: build                                 # run after build succeeds
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'          # conditional job
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with: { name: coverage }
keyPoints: Outputs are written to $GITHUB_OUTPUT; environment values go to $GITHUB_ENV; summaries to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY
Built-in caching in setup-* actions (cache: npm/pip/gradle/maven) is simpler than manual actions/cache
Use fail-fast: false when you want to see every combination's result
Artifacts are for sharing between jobs and downloading after the run; they are not a deployment target

concepts.name: Secrets, Variables, Environments & OIDC
concepts.explanation: Never hard-code credentials. Store secrets in GitHub, scope them to environments with approval rules, and — best of all — use OIDC so the workflow gets short-lived cloud credentials without storing any long-lived keys.
concepts.code:
# Context reference:  ${{ secrets.NAME }}   ${{ vars.NAME }}   ${{ github.sha }}
#
# Environment with required reviewers (Settings -> Environments -> production)
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production                # waits for approval; env-scoped secrets
    permissions:
      id-token: write                      # allow OIDC token request
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gha-deploy
          aws-region: ap-south-1
      - run: aws sts get-caller-identity
      - run: ./deploy.sh
        env:
          API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.API_TOKEN }}
keyPoints: OIDC trust policy on the cloud role restricts which repo, branch or environment may assume it
Secrets are masked in logs, but a malicious step can still exfiltrate them — only run trusted code
Be careful with pull_request_target and workflow_run: they run with secrets and can expose them to fork code
Use environments for approval gates and per-environment secrets (dev, staging, prod)

concepts.name: Docker Build & Push Pipeline
concepts.explanation: This is the most common real-world workflow: build an image on every push, tag it with the git SHA and branch, push it to a registry, and cache layers to stay fast. Metadata action generates consistent tags and labels.
concepts.code:
name: build-image
on:
  push: { branches: [main], tags: ["v*"] }
permissions: { contents: read, packages: write, id-token: write }
jobs:
  image:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - id: meta
        uses: docker/metadata-action@v6
        with:
          images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}
          tags: |
            type=sha
            type=ref,event=branch
            type=semver,pattern={{version}}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
          labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max
          platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
keyPoints: cache-from/to type=gha reuses layers between runs using the GitHub Actions cache
GITHUB_TOKEN with packages: write is enough for GHCR; no personal token needed
Add a Trivy scan step and fail the job on HIGH/CRITICAL vulnerabilities before pushing to production tags
Sign images with cosign (keyless using OIDC) and attach an SBOM

concepts.name: Reusable Workflows, Composite Actions & Self-Hosted Runners
concepts.explanation: Avoid copy-pasting pipelines. A reusable workflow (workflow_call) is a whole job template other repos can call; a composite action bundles several steps into one reusable step. Self-hosted runners let you run jobs inside your own network or on special hardware.
concepts.code:
# Reusable workflow  .github/workflows/deploy.yml (in a shared repo)
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      environment: { type: string, required: true }
    secrets:
      deploy_key: { required: true }
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: ${{ inputs.environment }}
    steps:
      - run: echo "Deploying to ${{ inputs.environment }}"

# Caller workflow
# jobs:
#   prod:
#     uses: myorg/platform/.github/workflows/deploy.yml@v1
#     with: { environment: production }
#     secrets: inherit
#
# Composite action: action.yml with  runs: { using: composite, steps: [...] }
# Self-hosted runner: runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, gpu]
#   -> use ephemeral runners (actions-runner-controller on Kubernetes) and never for public repos
keyPoints: Version your shared workflows with tags (@v1) so changes are controlled
Self-hosted runners on public repositories are a security risk; fork PRs could run arbitrary code
actions-runner-controller or runner autoscaling gives clean, ephemeral runners per job
Use paths filters and path-based triggers in monorepos to run only the affected pipelines

concepts.name: GitLab CI/CD Pipeline
concepts.explanation: GitLab CI is configured with a single .gitlab-ci.yml. You define stages, jobs, rules, caches and artifacts, and GitLab runners execute them. It has a built-in container registry, environments, and review apps, making it an all-in-one DevOps platform.
concepts.code:
# .gitlab-ci.yml
stages: [build, test, deploy]
default:
  image: node:24-alpine
  cache:
    key: { files: [package-lock.json] }
    paths: [node_modules/]
variables:
  DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR: "/certs"
build:
  stage: build
  script: [npm ci, npm run build]
  artifacts: { paths: [dist/], expire_in: 1 week }
test:
  stage: test
  script: [npm test]
  coverage: '/Lines\s*:\s*(\d+\.?\d*)%/'
docker-image:
  stage: build
  image: docker:27
  services: [docker:27-dind]
  script:
    - docker login -u $CI_REGISTRY_USER -p $CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD $CI_REGISTRY
    - docker build -t $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA .
    - docker push $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA
deploy-prod:
  stage: deploy
  script: ./deploy.sh
  environment: { name: production, url: https://app.example.com }
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"
      when: manual
keyPoints: Predefined variables like CI_COMMIT_SHA, CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE and CI_PIPELINE_ID are available in every job
rules: replaces only/except for deciding when jobs run; needs: builds a DAG instead of strict stages
Protected variables and protected branches control who can access production secrets
include: lets you reuse templates (SAST, dependency scanning) from GitLab or your own repo

concepts.name: Jenkins Declarative Pipeline
concepts.explanation: Jenkins is the long-standing, plugin-based automation server. A Jenkinsfile in the repository describes the pipeline in Groovy. It is flexible and widely used in enterprises, but needs more maintenance (plugins, upgrades, agents) than hosted CI.
keyPoints: Declarative syntax is preferred over scripted; use shared libraries for reusable code
Store secrets in the Jenkins credentials store and use withCredentials, never echo them
Run builds on ephemeral agents (Kubernetes plugin, Docker) not on the controller
Back up JENKINS_HOME and manage configuration as code (JCasC) so the server is reproducible

concepts.name: Choosing a CI/CD Tool
concepts.explanation: All popular tools do the same core job. Choose based on where your code lives, team skills, security needs and cost. In interviews, explain the trade-offs rather than declaring a favourite.
concepts.code:
# GitHub Actions  Best fit if code is on GitHub. Huge marketplace, YAML, OIDC, easy start.
# GitLab CI       All-in-one platform, strong built-in security + registry + environments.
# Jenkins         Maximum flexibility and plugins; self-managed; steeper maintenance.
# CircleCI        Fast hosted CI, good caching and parallelism.
# Azure DevOps    Strong Microsoft ecosystem + boards; pipelines in YAML.
# AWS CodePipeline/CodeBuild, Google Cloud Build   Native to a cloud, tight IAM integration.
# Tekton, Argo Workflows   Kubernetes-native pipelines.
# ArgoCD / Flux   Not CI: they are CD for Kubernetes via GitOps.
#
# Decision factors: hosting model, security/compliance, cost per minute,
# self-hosted runner needs, ecosystem/integrations, team familiarity, vendor lock-in
keyPoints: Keep pipeline logic in scripts (Makefile, shell, task) so migrating CI tools is easy
Managed SaaS CI reduces toil; self-hosted gives control and sometimes lower cost at scale
Separate CI (build/test) from CD (deploy) responsibilities when you adopt GitOps
Measure pipeline duration and success rate regardless of the tool

concepts.name: GitOps Principles
concepts.explanation: GitOps uses Git as the single source of truth for the desired state of infrastructure and applications. An agent inside the cluster continuously compares Git with reality and reconciles any difference. Deployments become pull requests, and rollbacks become git revert.
concepts.code:
# Four principles (OpenGitOps)
#  1. Declarative       desired state is expressed declaratively (YAML, Helm, Kustomize)
#  2. Versioned/immutable  state is stored in Git with full history
#  3. Pulled automatically an agent pulls changes (not CI pushing with cluster credentials)
#  4. Continuously reconciled  drift is detected and corrected
#
# Typical flow
#   dev pushes code -> CI builds image :sha -> CI opens PR/commit updating image tag in the
#   config repo -> reviewed + merged -> ArgoCD/Flux sees the change -> syncs the cluster
#
# Repos:  app repo (source code)  +  config/env repo (manifests per environment)
keyPoints: Pull-based deployments mean CI never needs admin credentials to the cluster, improving security
Every change is auditable in Git history; drift is visible and self-healing
Separate the app repository from the environment (config) repository
Secrets still must not be plain in Git — use SOPS, Sealed Secrets or External Secrets

concepts.name: Argo CD in Practice
concepts.explanation: Argo CD is a Kubernetes controller that syncs applications from Git. You define an Application resource pointing to a repo path and a destination cluster and namespace, and Argo shows sync and health status in a UI and CLI.
concepts.code:
# application.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata: { name: web, namespace: argocd }
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/myorg/config.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: apps/web/overlays/prod        # Kustomize/Helm/plain YAML
  destination: { server: https://kubernetes.default.svc, namespace: shop }
  syncPolicy:
    automated: { prune: true, selfHeal: true }     # delete removed, revert manual changes
    syncOptions: [CreateNamespace=true]
# CLI
# argocd login argocd.example.com --sso
# argocd app list
# argocd app sync web
# argocd app diff web
# argocd app history web;  argocd app rollback web <id>
# argocd app get web --refresh
keyPoints: selfHeal reverts manual kubectl edits; prune removes resources deleted from Git
ApplicationSets generate many Applications from a template (per cluster, per environment, per PR)
Use sync waves and hooks to order resources, run migrations, or smoke tests
Flux is the main alternative: GitRepository, Kustomization and HelmRelease custom resources do the same job

concepts.name: Progressive Delivery: Argo Rollouts & Flagger
concepts.explanation: Plain Deployments only offer rolling updates. Progressive delivery tools automate canary and blue/green releases, shift traffic gradually, analyse metrics, and roll back automatically when the new version looks unhealthy.
concepts.code:
# Argo Rollouts: replaces Deployment with a Rollout resource
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata: { name: web }
spec:
  replicas: 5
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
        - setWeight: 10
        - pause: { duration: 5m }
        - analysis: { templates: [{ templateName: error-rate-check }] }   # Prometheus query
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - setWeight: 100
# kubectl argo rollouts get rollout web --watch
# kubectl argo rollouts promote web
# kubectl argo rollouts abort web
keyPoints: Analysis templates query Prometheus (or Datadog) to decide automatically: promote, pause or abort
Traffic splitting needs support from an ingress, Gateway API implementation or service mesh
Keep canary steps short enough for fast delivery but long enough to gather meaningful metrics
Flagger offers the same idea and integrates with Flux, Istio, Linkerd and Gateway API

concepts.name: What IaC Is & Why It Matters
concepts.explanation: Infrastructure as Code means defining servers, networks, databases and permissions in version-controlled files instead of clicking in a console. The same code builds identical environments repeatedly, can be reviewed in pull requests, and can be rebuilt from scratch in a disaster.
concepts.code:
# Without IaC                          # With IaC
#  - manual clicks, undocumented        - everything in Git, reviewed, auditable
#  - "snowflake" environments           - dev/stage/prod from the same code
#  - slow, error-prone recovery         - rebuild an environment in minutes
#  - drift nobody notices               - drift detected by plan/refresh
#
# Declarative  (Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes YAML)
#   describe the END STATE; the tool works out the steps
# Imperative   (Bash scripts, AWS CLI, some Ansible tasks)
#   describe the STEPS to run, in order
#
# Idempotent: running it twice gives the same result as running it once
keyPoints: Idempotency and declarative style are the core ideas interviewers want to hear
IaC also enables policy-as-code, cost estimation and automated testing before apply
Treat infrastructure changes like application changes: branch, PR, plan review, apply
Manual console changes cause drift — lock down console write access in production

concepts.name: IaC Tool Landscape
concepts.explanation: There are several categories of tools, and most real projects combine them: provisioning (create the infrastructure), configuration management (configure the servers), and image building (bake machine images).
concepts.code:
# PROVISIONING (creates cloud resources)
#   Terraform / OpenTofu   multi-cloud, HCL, huge provider ecosystem
#   AWS CloudFormation / CDK    AWS-native (CDK = write it in TypeScript/Python/Java)
#   Pulumi                 real programming languages, multi-cloud
#   Azure Bicep / ARM      Azure-native      GCP Deployment Manager / Config Connector
#   Crossplane             manage cloud resources through Kubernetes APIs
#
# CONFIGURATION MANAGEMENT (configures what runs on servers)
#   Ansible (agentless, SSH, YAML)    Chef, Puppet (agent-based)    Salt
#
# IMAGE BUILDING
#   Packer (AMIs, VM images)     Docker/BuildKit (container images)    EC2 Image Builder
#
# KUBERNETES DEPLOYMENT
#   Helm, Kustomize, ArgoCD, Flux
keyPoints: Terraform for infrastructure, Ansible for configuration, Docker for packaging, Kubernetes for running is a classic stack
Containers and immutable images reduce the need for classic configuration management
OpenTofu is an open-source fork of Terraform under the Linux Foundation, mostly compatible
Choose one primary provisioning tool per organisation to avoid fragmentation

concepts.name: Drift, Immutable Infrastructure & Idempotency
concepts.explanation: Configuration drift happens when real infrastructure no longer matches the code, usually because of manual changes. Immutable infrastructure avoids it by replacing instead of modifying. Idempotent tools can be re-run safely at any time to converge on the desired state.
concepts.code:
# Detect drift
terraform plan -refresh-only             # shows differences between state and reality
terraform plan                           # shows what apply would change to match code
# Fix: either update the code to match reality, or apply to revert reality

# Idempotent vs non-idempotent
#   apt-get install -y nginx      idempotent (already installed = no change)
#   echo "line" >> /etc/file      NOT idempotent (appends every run)
#   ansible: lineinfile / package / service modules are idempotent by design
#
# Immutable pattern: Packer builds AMI v42 -> ASG launch template -> instance refresh
#   never SSH in to patch; build a new image and replace the instances
keyPoints: Scheduled terraform plan runs (with alerts) catch drift early
Use ignore_changes sparingly for attributes legitimately changed by other systems (e.g. autoscaling desired count)
Prefer ansible modules over raw shell/command tasks to keep playbooks idempotent
Immutable images give faster, safer rollbacks than patching in place

concepts.name: Terraform Core Workflow & Commands
concepts.explanation: Terraform describes infrastructure in HCL files. The loop is always the same: write code, init to download providers, plan to preview changes, apply to make them. The plan is your safety net — always read it. OpenTofu (the open-source fork) uses the same workflow with the tofu command.
concepts.code:
terraform version
terraform init                      # download providers/modules, set up the backend
terraform init -upgrade             # upgrade providers within constraints
terraform fmt -recursive            # canonical formatting
terraform validate                  # syntax + internal consistency
terraform plan -out=tfplan          # preview; save the plan
terraform show tfplan               # human-readable view of a saved plan
terraform apply tfplan              # apply EXACTLY the reviewed plan
terraform apply -auto-approve       # CI only; skips the prompt
terraform plan -target=aws_instance.web      # limit scope (use sparingly)
terraform plan -var="env=prod" -var-file=prod.tfvars
terraform destroy                   # delete everything managed by this state
terraform output; terraform output -raw db_endpoint
terraform graph | dot -Tsvg > graph.svg
terraform console                   # evaluate expressions interactively
terraform providers; terraform providers lock -platform=linux_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64
keyPoints: Commit .terraform.lock.hcl so everyone uses the same provider versions
plan -out then apply tfplan guarantees what was reviewed is what is applied
Never run terraform from a laptop against production when a pipeline exists
Use -target only for emergencies; it can leave state and code out of sync

concepts.name: HCL Building Blocks: Resources, Variables, Outputs, Locals, Data
concepts.explanation: Terraform code is made of a few block types. Resources create things, data sources read existing things, variables take input, locals hold computed values, and outputs expose results to people or other modules.
keyPoints: Reference other resources as resource_type.name.attribute — Terraform builds the dependency graph from references
Mark secrets sensitive = true, but remember they are still stored in plain text in the state file
Pin provider versions with ~> to avoid surprise breaking changes
Set values through terraform.tfvars, *.auto.tfvars, -var flags or TF_VAR_name environment variables

concepts.name: State, Remote Backends & Locking
concepts.explanation: Terraform records what it created in a state file. It maps your code to real resources and is essential for planning. Store state remotely with locking so teams cannot corrupt it by applying at the same time. Because state may contain secrets, protect it like a password.
concepts.code:
# backend.tf  - S3 backend with native state locking (Terraform 1.10+, OpenTofu 1.10+)
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "myorg-terraform-state"
    key          = "shop/prod/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "ap-south-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true          # S3 lock file; replaces the old dynamodb_table setting
  }
}
# Enable bucket versioning, block public access, restrict IAM to the CI role.
# Other backends: Terraform Cloud/HCP, GCS, Azure Blob, Postgres, Consul.
#
# State commands
#   terraform state list
#   terraform state show aws_instance.web
#   terraform state mv aws_instance.web aws_instance.app      # rename in state
#   terraform state rm aws_instance.web                       # stop managing (does not destroy)
#   terraform import aws_instance.web i-0abc123               # adopt an existing resource
#   terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>                          # only if a run crashed
#   terraform init -migrate-state                             # move to a new backend
keyPoints: Never edit the state file by hand and never commit it to Git
Split state per environment and per component to limit blast radius and speed up plans
DynamoDB-based locking is the legacy approach; native S3 locking removes the extra table
Import blocks (import { to = ..., id = ... }) let you adopt resources through code and plan

concepts.name: count, for_each, dynamic Blocks & Lifecycle
concepts.explanation: These language features create several similar resources and control how Terraform replaces them. for_each is usually better than count because items are keyed by name instead of by position.
keyPoints: Prefer for_each with a map or set; count is fine for simple on/off (count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0)
prevent_destroy on databases and state buckets blocks accidental deletion
depends_on adds an explicit dependency only when Terraform cannot infer one
moved blocks let you rename or restructure resources without destroying them

concepts.name: Modules & Project Structure
concepts.explanation: A module is a reusable folder of Terraform code with inputs (variables) and outputs. Use modules to package a pattern (VPC, EKS cluster, database) once and instantiate it for every environment, instead of copying code.
concepts.code:
# Recommended layout
# infra/
#   modules/
#     vpc/            main.tf variables.tf outputs.tf versions.tf README.md
#     eks/
#   envs/
#     dev/            main.tf backend.tf terraform.tfvars
#     prod/           main.tf backend.tf terraform.tfvars
#
# envs/prod/main.tf
module "vpc" {
  source  = "../../modules/vpc"        # local
  # source  = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"   # registry
  # version = "~> 6.0"
  name    = "shop-prod"
  cidr    = "10.0.0.0/16"
  azs     = ["ap-south-1a", "ap-south-1b"]
}
module "eks" {
  source     = "../../modules/eks"
  vpc_id     = module.vpc.vpc_id              # use another module's output
  subnet_ids = module.vpc.private_subnets
}
keyPoints: Keep modules small and focused, with documented variables and useful outputs
Pin registry or Git modules to a version so upgrades are deliberate
Directories per environment (or Terragrunt) are clearer and safer than workspaces for prod versus dev
Tools like Terragrunt reduce backend and variable repetition across many stacks

concepts.name: Workspaces, Testing, Policy & CI for Terraform
concepts.explanation: Workspaces give one configuration multiple state files, but real isolation between environments is usually better done with separate directories and backends. Around the core tool, a healthy pipeline adds linting, security scanning, cost estimation, policy checks and automated tests.
concepts.code:
terraform workspace list; terraform workspace new staging; terraform workspace select prod
# ${terraform.workspace} is available in code (use for small variations only)

# Quality tooling
tflint                                  # lint: invalid instance types, deprecated syntax
trivy config .                          # misconfiguration scan (replaces tfsec)
checkov -d .                            # policy/security scan for IaC
infracost breakdown --path .            # cost estimate on PRs
terraform test                          # native test framework (*.tftest.hcl)
# Policy as code: OPA/Conftest, Sentinel (Terraform Cloud), Checkov custom policies

# CI flow (pull request)
#   fmt -check -> validate -> tflint -> scan -> plan -> comment plan on the PR
# CI flow (merge to main)
#   plan -> manual approval for prod -> apply the saved plan
# Atlantis / Terraform Cloud / Spacelift / env0 / GitHub Actions run this for you
terraform fmt -check -recursive && terraform validate
keyPoints: Always post the plan output on the pull request for reviewers
Use OIDC roles for the pipeline, not static cloud keys
Run scheduled drift detection and alert on differences
OpenTofu adds features like state encryption; check compatibility before mixing the two tools in one project

concepts.name: Ansible Basics: Inventory, Ad-Hoc & Modules
concepts.explanation: Ansible configures servers over SSH with no agent to install. You list your hosts in an inventory, then run modules (small idempotent units like package, service, copy) either ad hoc from the command line or in playbooks.
concepts.code:
# inventory.ini
# [web]
# web1.example.com
# web2.example.com ansible_user=ubuntu
# [db]
# db1.example.com
# [prod:children]
# web
# db
# [all:vars]
# ansible_python_interpreter=/usr/bin/python3
ansible all -i inventory.ini -m ping
ansible web -i inventory.ini -m shell -a "uptime"
ansible web -b -m apt -a "name=nginx state=present update_cache=yes"   # -b = become (sudo)
ansible web -b -m service -a "name=nginx state=restarted"
ansible db -m copy -a "src=./backup.sh dest=/opt/backup.sh mode=0755"
ansible-inventory -i inventory.ini --graph
ansible-doc -l | grep -i ec2; ansible-doc apt       # built-in module docs
# Dynamic inventory: aws_ec2 plugin builds the host list from your cloud account
keyPoints: Ansible is agentless: it needs SSH access and Python on each target host (network devices are the exception)
Use ansible-doc to read module docs offline instead of searching the web
Prefer FQCNs in playbooks (ansible.builtin.apt) for clarity
Dynamic inventories keep host lists accurate in autoscaling environments

concepts.name: Playbooks, Handlers & Variables
concepts.explanation: A playbook is a YAML list of plays; each play targets hosts and runs ordered tasks. Handlers run only when notified by a change, which is how you restart a service only when its config actually changed.
concepts.code:
# site.yml
- name: Configure web servers
  hosts: web
  become: true
  vars:
    app_port: 8080
  tasks:
    - name: Install nginx
      ansible.builtin.apt:
        name: nginx
        state: present
        update_cache: true
    - name: Render nginx config from template
      ansible.builtin.template:
        src: nginx.conf.j2
        dest: /etc/nginx/conf.d/app.conf
        mode: "0644"
      notify: Reload nginx
    - name: Ensure nginx is running and enabled
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: started
        enabled: true
    - name: Only on Debian
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "{{ ansible_distribution }} {{ app_port }}"
      when: ansible_os_family == "Debian"
  handlers:
    - name: Reload nginx
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: reloaded
keyPoints: Run with: ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml
Useful flags: --check (dry run), --diff (show changes), --limit web1, --tags deploy, -v/-vvv, --start-at-task
Loops: loop: "{{ packages }}"; conditionals: when:; register: saves a task result for later tasks
Templates use Jinja2: {{ variable }}, {% if %}, filters like | default('x')

concepts.name: Roles, Vault & Galaxy
concepts.explanation: Roles organise playbooks into reusable units with a standard folder layout. Ansible Vault encrypts sensitive variables so secrets can live in Git safely, and Galaxy shares community roles and collections.
concepts.code:
# roles/nginx/
#   tasks/main.yml  handlers/main.yml  templates/  files/  defaults/main.yml  vars/main.yml  meta/main.yml
# Using a role
# - hosts: web
#   roles:
#     - role: nginx
#       vars: { nginx_port: 8080 }
ansible-galaxy init roles/nginx
ansible-galaxy collection install amazon.aws community.general
ansible-galaxy install -r requirements.yml

# Vault
ansible-vault create group_vars/prod/vault.yml
ansible-vault encrypt secrets.yml; ansible-vault decrypt secrets.yml
ansible-vault edit group_vars/prod/vault.yml
ansible-playbook site.yml --ask-vault-pass
ansible-playbook site.yml --vault-password-file ~/.vault_pass    # CI: from a secret

ansible-lint site.yml
molecule test               # test roles in containers
keyPoints: Variable precedence is a classic gotcha: role defaults are lowest, extra vars (-e) are highest
Keep encrypted vars in a separate file from plain vars so diffs stay readable
ansible-lint and molecule give roles the same discipline as application code
For Kubernetes-based infrastructure, Ansible is often used for node/bootstrap tasks and Terraform for cloud resources

concepts.name: Secrets Management Principles
concepts.explanation: A secret (password, API key, certificate, token) must never live in source code, container images, CI logs or chat. Store them in a dedicated secret manager, inject them at runtime, rotate them regularly, and give each service only the secrets it needs.
concepts.code:
# Rules
#  1. Never commit secrets (use .gitignore + pre-commit hooks: gitleaks, detect-secrets)
#  2. Prefer short-lived, dynamically issued credentials (Vault, cloud IAM, OIDC)
#  3. Use workload identity, not static keys:  IRSA (EKS), Workload Identity (GKE),
#     Managed Identity (Azure), IAM roles for EC2/ECS/Lambda
#  4. Encrypt at rest and in transit; audit every access
#  5. Rotate on a schedule and immediately after exposure
#  6. Least privilege per service; separate secrets per environment
#
# If a secret was committed: REVOKE/ROTATE FIRST, then clean history
# (git filter-repo / BFG) - removing it from Git alone does not make it safe
gitleaks detect --source . --verbose
pre-commit install
keyPoints: Rotating a leaked secret is mandatory; deleting the commit is not enough because copies exist
Environment variables are convenient but visible in process listings and crash dumps
Make rotation a non-event by using managed rotation (Secrets Manager rotation lambdas, Vault dynamic secrets)
Security scanning of repos and CI logs should be automatic

concepts.name: Secret Managers: Vault, AWS Secrets Manager & SSM
concepts.explanation: Dedicated secret stores add encryption, access policies, audit logs and rotation. HashiCorp Vault is cloud-agnostic and can generate dynamic credentials; cloud providers offer native managers that integrate with IAM.
concepts.code:
# AWS
aws secretsmanager create-secret --name prod/db --secret-string '{"user":"app","password":"S3cret"}'
aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id prod/db --query SecretString --output text
aws ssm put-parameter --name /prod/app/api_key --type SecureString --value "abc123"
aws ssm get-parameter --name /prod/app/api_key --with-decryption --query Parameter.Value --output text
# Parameter Store: cheap, hierarchical config.  Secrets Manager: built-in rotation, higher cost.

# HashiCorp Vault
export VAULT_ADDR=https://vault.example.com
vault login -method=oidc
vault kv put secret/shop/prod db_password=S3cret
vault kv get -field=db_password secret/shop/prod
vault read database/creds/readonly          # dynamic, short-lived DB user
vault policy write app-read policy.hcl
# Other: Azure Key Vault, Google Secret Manager, Doppler, 1Password Connect
keyPoints: Vault dynamic secrets create a unique credential per request that expires automatically
Use KMS (AWS KMS, Cloud KMS) for envelope encryption of data and keys
Grant access by IAM role/identity, not by passing a shared token around
Enable audit logging so you can answer who read which secret and when

concepts.name: Secrets in Git & Kubernetes: SOPS, Sealed Secrets, External Secrets
concepts.explanation: GitOps wants everything in Git, but secrets must not be plain text. There are two common patterns: encrypt the secret inside the repo (SOPS, Sealed Secrets), or keep it in a secret manager and sync it into the cluster (External Secrets Operator, Secrets Store CSI).
concepts.code:
# SOPS: encrypts only the values of YAML/JSON using KMS/age/PGP; file stays diff-friendly
sops --encrypt --kms arn:aws:kms:ap-south-1:123456789012:key/abcd secrets.yaml > secrets.enc.yaml
sops --decrypt secrets.enc.yaml
sops secrets.enc.yaml                       # edit in place (decrypt -> editor -> re-encrypt)

# Sealed Secrets: encrypt with the cluster's public key; only the controller can decrypt
kubeseal --format yaml < secret.yaml > sealed-secret.yaml     # safe to commit

# External Secrets Operator: reference a store, get a native K8s Secret
# apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
# kind: ExternalSecret
# metadata: { name: db }
# spec:
#   refreshInterval: 1h
#   secretStoreRef: { name: aws-secrets, kind: ClusterSecretStore }
#   target: { name: db }
#   data:
#   - secretKey: password
#     remoteRef: { key: prod/db, property: password }
keyPoints: External Secrets keeps the single source of truth in the secret manager and handles rotation automatically
SOPS works well for Terraform, Helm values and ArgoCD with plugins (helm-secrets, KSOPS)
Enable Kubernetes encryption at rest and restrict who can read Secrets via RBAC
Always prefer workload identity so the cluster authenticates to the secret store without static keys

concepts.name: Cloud Service Models & Shared Responsibility
concepts.explanation: Cloud services come in layers. IaaS gives you raw virtual machines and networks, PaaS gives you a managed runtime, FaaS runs individual functions, and SaaS is a finished application. The higher the layer, the less you manage and the less control you have. In every model the provider secures the cloud itself, while you secure what you put in it.
concepts.code:
#             YOU manage                                  PROVIDER manages
# On-prem     everything
# IaaS        OS, runtime, app, data                      hardware, virtualisation, network   (EC2, Azure VM, GCE)
# CaaS        container workloads                         cluster control plane/nodes          (EKS, GKE, AKS, ECS)
# PaaS        app code + data                             OS, runtime, scaling                 (Elastic Beanstalk, App Service, Cloud Run, Heroku)
# FaaS        function code                               everything else, scales to zero      (Lambda, Azure Functions, Cloud Functions)
# SaaS        configuration + users                       the whole application                (Gmail, Salesforce, GitHub)
#
# Shared responsibility
#   Provider: security OF the cloud   (datacentres, hardware, hypervisor, managed-service internals)
#   You:      security IN the cloud   (IAM, data, network rules, OS patches on VMs, app code)
keyPoints: Most cloud breaches come from customer misconfiguration (public buckets, open ports, leaked keys), not provider failure
Public, private, hybrid and multi-cloud describe where workloads run; multi-cloud adds complexity, so justify it
Pay-as-you-go turns capital expense into operating expense and enables elasticity
Know one cloud deeply and understand the equivalent services in the others

concepts.name: Regions, Availability Zones & High Availability
concepts.explanation: A region is a geographic area; an availability zone (AZ) is one or more isolated data centres inside it. Spreading workloads across at least two AZs protects against a data centre failure; using multiple regions protects against a regional failure and reduces latency for global users.
concepts.code:
# Region           ap-south-1 (Mumbai)      -> pick for latency, data residency, price, services
# Availability Zone  ap-south-1a / 1b / 1c  -> separate power, cooling, networking, low-latency links
# Edge locations     CDN / DNS points of presence worldwide
#
# HA pattern (single region)
#   Route 53 / DNS -> ALB (spans AZs) -> app instances in AZ-a + AZ-b (ASG) -> RDS Multi-AZ
#
# DR strategies (cost and speed rise together)
#   Backup & restore        RPO hours, RTO hours     cheapest
#   Pilot light             minimal core running in DR region
#   Warm standby            scaled-down copy always running
#   Active-active multi-region   RPO/RTO near zero   most expensive
#
# RPO = max acceptable data loss (time).  RTO = max acceptable downtime.
keyPoints: Design for failure: assume any single instance, AZ or dependency can disappear
Multi-AZ gives high availability; cross-region replication gives disaster recovery
Data transfer between AZs and regions costs money — factor it into design
Test failover regularly; an untested DR plan is only a hope

concepts.name: IAM Fundamentals: Users, Roles, Policies
concepts.explanation: Identity and Access Management controls who (identity) can do what (actions) on which resources. The golden rules: least privilege, no long-lived keys, roles instead of users for workloads, MFA for humans. IAM mistakes are the most common cause of serious cloud incidents.
concepts.code:
# Core concepts (AWS names; Azure RBAC and GCP IAM are similar)
#   User / SSO identity   a human           Group   set of users
#   Role                  assumable identity with temporary credentials (EC2, Lambda, CI, other accounts)
#   Policy                JSON document: Effect, Action, Resource, Condition
#
# Example: read-only to one S3 bucket
# {
#   "Version": "2012-10-17",
#   "Statement": [{
#     "Effect": "Allow",
#     "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:ListBucket"],
#     "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket", "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*"]
#   }]
# }
# Evaluation: explicit DENY > explicit ALLOW > default deny
# Policy types: identity-based, resource-based (bucket policy), permission boundary, SCP (org-wide guardrail)
aws sts get-caller-identity               # who am I right now?
aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn <arn> --action-names s3:GetObject
keyPoints: Workloads should assume roles (instance profile, IRSA, task role) rather than embed access keys
Use separate accounts/projects per environment and a central landing zone (AWS Organizations, Control Tower)
Enforce MFA and SSO (IAM Identity Center) for people; disable the root account for daily use
Access Analyzer and credential reports find unused or overly broad permissions

concepts.name: Core Services Cheat Table: AWS vs Azure vs GCP
concepts.explanation: Knowing the equivalent service names across clouds is helpful for interviews and multi-cloud teams. The concepts are the same; only the names and some limits differ.
concepts.code:
# CAPABILITY          AWS                    AZURE                    GCP
# Virtual machines    EC2                    Virtual Machines         Compute Engine
# Autoscaling VMs     Auto Scaling Group     VM Scale Sets            Managed Instance Group
# Containers (K8s)    EKS                    AKS                      GKE
# Containers (simple) ECS / Fargate          Container Apps / ACI     Cloud Run
# Serverless func     Lambda                 Functions                Cloud Functions / Cloud Run
# Object storage      S3                     Blob Storage             Cloud Storage
# Block storage       EBS                    Managed Disks            Persistent Disk
# File storage        EFS                    Azure Files              Filestore
# Relational DB       RDS / Aurora           SQL Database / Flexible  Cloud SQL / AlloyDB
# NoSQL               DynamoDB               Cosmos DB                Firestore / Bigtable
# Cache               ElastiCache            Azure Cache for Redis    Memorystore
# Queue / pub-sub     SQS / SNS / EventBridge Service Bus / Event Grid Pub/Sub
# Load balancer       ALB / NLB              App Gateway / LB         Cloud Load Balancing
# DNS / CDN           Route 53 / CloudFront  Azure DNS / Front Door   Cloud DNS / Cloud CDN
# Private network     VPC                    VNet                     VPC
# IAM                 IAM / Identity Center  Entra ID + RBAC          Cloud IAM
# Secrets / keys      Secrets Manager / KMS  Key Vault                Secret Manager / Cloud KMS
# Registry            ECR                    ACR                      Artifact Registry
# Monitoring          CloudWatch             Azure Monitor            Cloud Monitoring
# IaC native          CloudFormation / CDK   Bicep / ARM              Deployment Manager / Terraform
keyPoints: Learn the concept first (object storage, managed Kubernetes), then the vendor name
AWS has the largest market share; Azure dominates in Microsoft-heavy enterprises; GCP is strong in data and Kubernetes
Managed services reduce toil but can raise cost and lock-in
Free tiers and sandbox accounts are the best way to practise safely

concepts.name: Well-Architected Pillars
concepts.explanation: Major clouds publish a framework of design principles. The AWS Well-Architected Framework has six pillars, and most review questions map to them. Use them as a checklist when designing or reviewing any system.
concepts.code:
# 1. Operational Excellence  automate, small reversible changes, learn from failure, runbooks
# 2. Security                least privilege, defence in depth, encrypt everything, traceability
# 3. Reliability             multi-AZ, health checks, auto-recovery, tested backups, limits management
# 4. Performance Efficiency  right-size, use managed/serverless, measure, cache
# 5. Cost Optimisation       pay for what you use, rightsizing, savings plans, tagging, shut down idle
# 6. Sustainability          efficient resources, region choice, utilisation, reduce waste
#
# Quick design questions
#   What is the single point of failure?      What is the blast radius of one bad deploy?
#   How do we know it is broken (alerts)?     How fast can we recover (RTO/RPO)?
#   Who has access and why?                   What does it cost per month at 10x traffic?
keyPoints: Frameworks give you vocabulary to justify trade-offs in system design interviews
Cost, security and reliability are constantly in tension — state your priorities explicitly
Review architecture regularly, not only at launch
Tag everything (team, env, cost-centre) from day one; tagging powers cost and ownership reports

concepts.name: AWS CLI Setup, Profiles & SSO
concepts.explanation: The AWS CLI v2 is the scripting interface to everything in AWS. Configure named profiles for each account, prefer SSO (short-lived credentials) over static access keys, and always verify which identity you are using before running changes.
concepts.code:
aws --version
aws configure                                   # access key, secret, region, output (legacy style)
aws configure sso                               # recommended: IAM Identity Center
aws sso login --profile prod
aws configure list; aws configure list-profiles
export AWS_PROFILE=prod AWS_REGION=ap-south-1
aws sts get-caller-identity                     # ALWAYS check account + role first
aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/Admin --role-session-name me

# ~/.aws/config
# [profile prod]
# sso_session = company
# sso_account_id = 123456789012
# sso_role_name = Developer
# region = ap-south-1
# output = json
#
# Helpers
aws ec2 describe-regions --query 'Regions[].RegionName' --output text
aws <service> help; aws <service> <command> help
aws ... --dry-run                               # supported by many EC2 calls
keyPoints: Credential lookup order: CLI flags, environment variables, profile, container/instance role
Never commit ~/.aws/credentials or paste access keys into scripts and chat
--output table|json|text|yaml and --no-cli-pager make scripts friendlier
On servers use instance roles; they provide automatically rotated credentials

concepts.name: Querying & Filtering CLI Output (JMESPath & jq)
concepts.explanation: AWS responses are large JSON documents. The built-in --query option uses JMESPath to extract exactly the fields you need server-side, while jq gives more flexible post-processing. This is the key to useful AWS scripting.
concepts.code:
# --query (JMESPath)
aws ec2 describe-instances --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].InstanceId' --output text
aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --filters "Name=tag:Env,Values=prod" "Name=instance-state-name,Values=running" \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].{ID:InstanceId,IP:PrivateIpAddress,Name:Tags[?Key==`Name`]|[0].Value}' \
  --output table
aws s3api list-buckets --query 'Buckets[?starts_with(Name, `prod-`)].Name'
aws ec2 describe-volumes --query 'Volumes[?State==`available`].[VolumeId,Size]' --output text   # unattached volumes = wasted cost

# Server-side --filters vs client-side --query:
#   --filters reduces what AWS returns (faster); --query reshapes the result

# jq for more complex logic
aws iam list-users | jq -r '.Users[] | select(.PasswordLastUsed == null) | .UserName'

# Pagination
aws s3api list-objects-v2 --bucket my-bucket --max-items 1000
aws ... --no-paginate
# Waiters
aws ec2 wait instance-running --instance-ids i-0abc
keyPoints: Use backticks around literals in JMESPath filters (`prod`)
Combine --filters for efficiency with --query for formatting
Waiters (aws ec2 wait ...) make scripts reliable instead of sleeping blindly
Output text with query is ideal to feed shell loops

concepts.name: EC2, EBS & Auto Scaling Commands
concepts.explanation: EC2 gives virtual servers. Prefer launching them from a launch template inside an Auto Scaling Group rather than by hand. These commands cover inspecting, starting, stopping and connecting to instances.
concepts.code:
aws ec2 describe-instances --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,State.Name,InstanceType,PrivateIpAddress]' --output table
aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-0abc --instance-type t3.micro --key-name mykey \
  --security-group-ids sg-0abc --subnet-id subnet-0abc \
  --iam-instance-profile Name=app-role --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=web}]'
aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-0abc
aws ec2 start-instances --instance-ids i-0abc
aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids i-0abc           # destructive

# Connect without opening port 22 (SSM Session Manager)
aws ssm start-session --target i-0abc
aws ssm send-command --document-name AWS-RunShellScript --targets Key=tag:Env,Values=prod --parameters 'commands=["uptime"]'

# Snapshots and AMIs
aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id vol-0abc --description "pre-upgrade"
aws ec2 create-image --instance-id i-0abc --name "web-v42" --no-reboot

# Auto Scaling
aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-groups --query 'AutoScalingGroups[].[AutoScalingGroupName,DesiredCapacity]'
aws autoscaling set-desired-capacity --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg --desired-capacity 4
aws autoscaling start-instance-refresh --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg
keyPoints: Session Manager gives audited shell access without SSH keys or open inbound ports
Stopped instances still pay for EBS volumes and Elastic IPs
IMDSv2 (token-required instance metadata) should be enforced to reduce SSRF credential theft
Use instance refresh in an ASG to roll out a new AMI safely

concepts.name: S3, IAM & Networking Commands
concepts.explanation: S3 is object storage used for artifacts, backups, static sites and data lakes. High-level aws s3 commands cover everyday use; aws s3api exposes the full API. Also learn the basic IAM and VPC inspection commands.
concepts.code:
aws s3 ls; aws s3 ls s3://my-bucket/logs/ --recursive --human-readable --summarize
aws s3 cp file.txt s3://my-bucket/; aws s3 cp s3://my-bucket/file.txt .
aws s3 sync ./dist s3://my-site --delete                  # deploy a static site
aws s3 sync s3://src s3://dst
aws s3 rm s3://my-bucket/old/ --recursive
aws s3 presign s3://my-bucket/report.pdf --expires-in 3600   # temporary download URL
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket my-bucket --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled
aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket my-bucket --public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true

# IAM
aws iam list-roles --query 'Roles[].RoleName'
aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name app-role --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess
aws iam create-access-key --user-name ci-user      # avoid; prefer roles/OIDC

# VPC
aws ec2 describe-vpcs; aws ec2 describe-subnets --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-0abc
aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids sg-0abc
aws ec2 describe-route-tables; aws ec2 describe-nat-gateways
keyPoints: Block Public Access should be on by default for every bucket unless it is a deliberate website
Enable versioning and lifecycle rules (transition to cheaper tiers, expire old data)
Encrypt buckets (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS) and log access for sensitive data
sync --delete mirrors the source exactly: run it with --dryrun first

concepts.name: Containers, Databases, Logs & Serverless on AWS
concepts.explanation: The services that most DevOps teams touch weekly: container registry and orchestration, managed databases, logging, and Lambda. The commands below handle the common operational tasks.
concepts.code:
# ECR + ECS + EKS
aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin <acct>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com
aws ecs list-clusters; aws ecs list-services --cluster prod
aws ecs update-service --cluster prod --service api --force-new-deployment
aws ecs execute-command --cluster prod --task <id> --container app --interactive --command "/bin/sh"
aws eks update-kubeconfig --name prod-cluster --region ap-south-1     # configure kubectl
aws eks list-clusters; aws eks describe-cluster --name prod-cluster

# RDS
aws rds describe-db-instances --query 'DBInstances[].[DBInstanceIdentifier,DBInstanceStatus,MultiAZ]'
aws rds create-db-snapshot --db-instance-identifier prod-db --db-snapshot-identifier pre-migration
aws rds reboot-db-instance --db-instance-identifier prod-db --force-failover   # test Multi-AZ failover

# CloudWatch Logs
aws logs tail /aws/lambda/my-func --follow --since 1h
aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name /ecs/api --filter-pattern "ERROR" --start-time $(date -d '1 hour ago' +%s000)
aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --state-value ALARM

# Lambda
aws lambda invoke --function-name my-func --payload '{"a":1}' --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out out.json
aws lambda update-function-code --function-name my-func --zip-file fileb://function.zip
keyPoints: aws eks update-kubeconfig is the standard way to get kubectl access to an EKS cluster
aws logs tail --follow is a quick alternative to opening the console for live logs
Take a snapshot before risky database changes; test restores, not just backups
ECS Exec and SSM remove the need for SSH into containers or instances

concepts.name: VMs vs Containers vs Serverless vs PaaS
concepts.explanation: There is no single best compute platform. Pick the simplest option that meets your needs: PaaS or serverless for small teams and simple apps, containers on a managed orchestrator for microservices, Kubernetes when you need its ecosystem and portability, and VMs for legacy or special requirements.
concepts.code:
# OPTION               BEST FOR                              TRADE-OFF
# VMs (EC2/GCE)        legacy apps, full control, GPUs       you patch, scale and secure the OS
# PaaS (App Runner,    web apps/APIs with minimal ops        less control, platform limits
#  Cloud Run, Beanstalk,
#  App Service, Heroku)
# Containers on ECS/   microservices without managing K8s    cloud-specific orchestration
#  Fargate/Container Apps
# Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/ portability, rich ecosystem,         steep learning curve, operational overhead
#  AKS)                large multi-team platforms
# Serverless functions event-driven, spiky traffic, glue     cold starts, time limits, vendor lock-in,
#  (Lambda)                                                  hard local debugging
# Static hosting + CDN (S3+CloudFront, Vercel, Netlify, GitHub Pages)   front ends, docs, sites
#
# Rule of thumb: start with the least-managed-by-you option that works,
# move up only when you hit its limits.
keyPoints: Kubernetes is powerful but is a platform you must operate; do not adopt it for one small app
Serverless shines for bursty or event-driven work and costs near zero when idle
Consider team skills and on-call burden, not only technical fit
Containerise early: it keeps every later platform choice open

concepts.name: Static Sites & Frontend Deployment
concepts.explanation: Frontend apps built into static files (React, Vue, Angular, docs) can be served from object storage behind a CDN, or from specialised platforms. This is cheap, fast and scales automatically. This very app is deployed this way on GitHub Pages.
concepts.code:
# Build to static files
npm ci && npm run build            # output: dist/ or build/

# Option A: S3 + CloudFront
aws s3 sync dist/ s3://my-site-bucket --delete --cache-control "public,max-age=31536000,immutable" --exclude index.html
aws s3 cp dist/index.html s3://my-site-bucket/index.html --cache-control "no-cache"
aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id E123ABC --paths "/index.html"

# Option B: GitHub Pages via Actions   (upload-pages-artifact + deploy-pages)
# Option C: Vercel / Netlify / Cloudflare Pages   (connect repo; push = deploy; PR previews)
# SPA routing: serve index.html for unknown paths (CloudFront custom error response,
#   nginx try_files, or copy index.html to every route on hosts without rewrites)
keyPoints: Cache hashed asset files for a long time; never cache index.html aggressively
Invalidate the CDN only for files that changed without a new filename
Single-page apps need a fallback to index.html so deep links do not return 404
Use preview deployments per pull request to review UI changes

concepts.name: Azure CLI (az) Essentials
concepts.explanation: The Azure CLI manages Azure resources through resource groups — logical containers for related resources. Authenticate, choose a subscription, and then create, query and delete resources. The commands follow the pattern az <service> <noun> <verb>.
concepts.code:
az login; az account list -o table
az account set --subscription "Prod-Subscription"
az group create -n rg-shop-prod -l centralindia
az group list -o table; az group delete -n rg-shop-dev --yes --no-wait   # deletes everything inside

az vm create -g rg-shop-prod -n web1 --image Ubuntu2404 --size Standard_B2s --admin-username azureuser --generate-ssh-keys
az vm list -d -o table; az vm start|stop|deallocate -g rg-shop-prod -n web1
az aks create -g rg-shop-prod -n shop-aks --node-count 3 --enable-managed-identity --generate-ssh-keys
az aks get-credentials -g rg-shop-prod -n shop-aks          # configure kubectl
az acr login --name myregistry; az acr build -t api:1.0 -r myregistry .
az storage account create -n shopstore123 -g rg-shop-prod --sku Standard_LRS
az keyvault secret set --vault-name shop-kv --name db-password --value 'S3cret'
az webapp up --name shop-web --runtime "NODE:22-lts"
az resource list -g rg-shop-prod -o table
az ... --query "[].{name:name,state:powerState}" -o table     # JMESPath, like AWS
keyPoints: Deallocate (not just stop) a VM to stop paying for compute
Use Entra ID managed identities instead of storing credentials
Bicep (az deployment group create) is the native IaC option; Terraform works well too
az interactive and az find help discover commands

concepts.name: Google Cloud CLI (gcloud) Essentials
concepts.explanation: gcloud manages Google Cloud through projects. Authenticate, set the active project and region, then work with services. GKE and Cloud Run are the most common DevOps targets.
concepts.code:
gcloud auth login; gcloud auth application-default login
gcloud projects list; gcloud config set project my-project
gcloud config set compute/region asia-south1
gcloud config list; gcloud config configurations list      # named config sets

gcloud compute instances create web1 --machine-type=e2-medium --zone=asia-south1-a --image-family=debian-12 --image-project=debian-cloud
gcloud compute instances list; gcloud compute ssh web1 --zone=asia-south1-a
gcloud container clusters create-auto prod --region=asia-south1      # GKE Autopilot
gcloud container clusters get-credentials prod --region=asia-south1
gcloud run deploy api --image=asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-project/repo/api:1.0 --region=asia-south1 --allow-unauthenticated
gcloud run services list; gcloud run services update-traffic api --to-revisions=api-00002=10   # canary
gcloud artifacts repositories list
gsutil ls gs://my-bucket;  gcloud storage cp file gs://my-bucket/      # gcloud storage is the modern CLI
gcloud secrets create db-pass --data-file=pass.txt
gcloud logging read "resource.type=cloud_run_revision AND severity>=ERROR" --limit=20
gcloud iam service-accounts list
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding my-project --member="serviceAccount:ci@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com" --role="roles/run.admin"
