keyPoints: Interview the company too: you will live with its on-call and tooling for years
Ask for the tech stack in advance so you can revise relevant commands
Send a short thank-you note summarising your interest and one thing you learned
Negotiate on total package including on-call pay, learning budget and remote policy

concepts.name: Q: What is DevOps and why do companies adopt it?
concepts.explanation: DevOps is a set of cultural practices, processes and tools that unite development and operations so software is delivered faster and more reliably. Companies adopt it to shorten lead time from idea to production, reduce failed releases and recovery time, and increase collaboration by giving teams shared ownership of what they build and run.
keyPoints: Mention the loop: plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate, monitor, then feedback
Key outcomes: faster deploys, fewer failures, quicker recovery — measurable with DORA metrics
Say it is culture first, tools second
Example: replacing manual quarterly releases with automated daily deployments

concepts.name: Q: What are the DORA metrics and how would you improve them?
concepts.explanation: DORA metrics measure delivery performance: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to restore service. To improve them I would first measure the baseline from CI/CD and incident data, then remove the largest bottleneck — for example slow pipelines and large batch sizes for lead time, or missing tests and canary releases for failure rate.
keyPoints: Speed metrics: deployment frequency and lead time; stability metrics: change failure rate and MTTR
Improvement levers: trunk-based development, small PRs, test automation, feature flags, fast rollback
Never use the metrics to compare or punish individuals
Speed and stability improve together in elite teams

concepts.name: Q: What is the difference between Agile and DevOps?
concepts.explanation: Agile is a way of planning and building software in short iterations with frequent customer feedback, focused mainly on development. DevOps extends that idea across the full lifecycle by automating build, test, release and operations and by merging development and operations responsibility. Agile gets the right software built quickly; DevOps gets it safely into production and keeps it running.
keyPoints: Agile: sprints, user stories, retrospectives; DevOps: CI/CD, IaC, monitoring, on-call
They complement each other; most DevOps teams also work in Agile ways
DevOps removes the "deployment wall" Agile alone does not address
SRE and platform engineering are specialisations that implement DevOps goals

concepts.name: Q: What is the difference between DevOps and SRE?
concepts.explanation: DevOps is a broad culture and set of practices, while SRE (Site Reliability Engineering) is a specific engineering discipline from Google that applies software engineering to operations problems. SRE uses concrete tools — SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, toil limits — to make reliability measurable, so it is often described as one opinionated implementation of DevOps.
keyPoints: DevOps answers "how do we collaborate and deliver faster?"; SRE answers "how reliable should it be and how do we prove it?"
SRE teams cap toil at roughly 50% and use error budgets to balance features against stability
In small companies one DevOps engineer often does both jobs
"class SRE implements DevOps" is a well-known summary

concepts.name: Q: What is Infrastructure as Code and what are its benefits?
concepts.explanation: Infrastructure as Code defines infrastructure in version-controlled configuration files that tools like Terraform or CloudFormation apply automatically. Benefits are repeatability, consistency across environments, peer review through pull requests, an audit trail, faster provisioning, and the ability to rebuild everything quickly after a disaster.
keyPoints: Declarative tools describe the desired end state; imperative scripts describe steps
Eliminates configuration drift and undocumented "snowflake" servers
Enables testing, policy-as-code and cost estimation before changes are applied
Examples: Terraform, Pulumi, CloudFormation, Ansible

concepts.name: Q: What does "shift left" mean?
concepts.explanation: Shift left means moving activities like testing, security scanning and quality checks earlier in the development lifecycle, to the left on a timeline, so defects are found when they are cheapest to fix. In practice it means unit tests, linting, secret scanning, SAST and dependency checks run on every commit or pull request rather than just before release.
keyPoints: Cost of fixing a bug grows dramatically the later it is found
Examples: pre-commit hooks, PR checks, IaC scanning, threat modelling during design
Balance: checks must be fast and low-noise or developers bypass them
DevSecOps is shift-left applied to security

concepts.name: Q: What is the difference between continuous integration, continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
concepts.explanation: Continuous integration automatically builds and tests every change merged into a shared branch. Continuous delivery extends that so the main branch is always in a releasable state and deployment to production needs only a manual approval. Continuous deployment removes the approval, so every change that passes all automated checks is released to production automatically.
keyPoints: CI = integrate often; CD (delivery) = always deployable; CD (deployment) = automatically deployed
Continuous deployment needs strong tests, monitoring and fast rollback
Many regulated companies choose delivery with an approval gate
Always clarify which "CD" the interviewer means

concepts.name: Q: What are pets vs cattle, and what is immutable infrastructure?
concepts.explanation: Pets are unique, hand-maintained servers that you repair when they fail; cattle are identical, disposable servers that you replace automatically. Immutable infrastructure applies this idea fully: you never modify a running server, you build a new image and replace the old instances. It prevents configuration drift and makes rollbacks reliable.
keyPoints: Examples: AMIs built with Packer, Docker images, Kubernetes pods
Mutable infra relies on patching or configuring servers in place
State (databases, volumes) is the exception and must be managed separately
Benefit: what you tested is exactly what runs in production

concepts.name: Q: How do you handle configuration and secrets across environments?
concepts.explanation: I keep the same build artifact for every environment and inject configuration at runtime through environment variables, ConfigMaps or a config service, following the twelve-factor approach. Secrets are stored in a secret manager such as Vault or AWS Secrets Manager, delivered through workload identity or an operator like External Secrets, rotated regularly, and never committed to Git or baked into images.
keyPoints: Different values per environment, same image and code
Use SOPS or Sealed Secrets if secrets must live in Git (encrypted)
Scan repositories with gitleaks and use pre-commit hooks
If a secret leaks: rotate immediately, then clean history

concepts.name: Q: What is a blameless postmortem and why is it important?
concepts.explanation: A blameless postmortem is a written review after an incident that focuses on how systems, processes and decisions allowed the failure instead of blaming a person. It records the timeline, impact, root and contributing causes, what went well and badly, and tracked action items. Blamelessness encourages honest reporting, which is the only way an organisation learns and prevents repeat incidents.
keyPoints: People act reasonably with the information they had; fix the system that made the mistake easy
Always end with owned, dated action items
Share postmortems widely to spread learning
Related metrics: MTTD, MTTR, incident frequency

concepts.name: Q: How do you decide which tool to use for a problem?
concepts.explanation: I start from the requirement and constraints — scale, team skills, security and compliance, existing ecosystem, cost, and operational burden — then compare two or three options and prototype the riskiest assumption. I prefer simple, well-supported tools that the team can operate, and I weigh managed services against self-hosting by the on-call burden they add.
keyPoints: Avoid resume-driven choices (do not run Kubernetes for one small app)
Consider lock-in, community, documentation and hiring
Make the decision visible in an ADR (architecture decision record)
Re-evaluate when requirements change

concepts.name: Q: What is a DevOps engineer's day-to-day work?
concepts.explanation: It typically includes maintaining CI/CD pipelines, managing infrastructure as code, supporting deployments and Kubernetes clusters, monitoring and responding to alerts, improving reliability and cost, automating repetitive tasks, reviewing pull requests for infrastructure, and helping developers with tooling and environments. The mix depends on company size: smaller teams cover everything, larger ones split into platform, SRE and security roles.
keyPoints: Core themes: automate, observe, secure, enable developers
On-call and incident response are part of the job in most companies
Collaboration and documentation matter as much as scripting
Be honest about which parts you have done hands-on

concepts.name: Q: What happens when you type a URL in the browser and press Enter?
concepts.explanation: The browser checks its caches, then resolves the domain through DNS to an IP address. It opens a TCP connection with a three-way handshake, performs a TLS handshake for HTTPS to verify the certificate and agree on encryption keys, and sends an HTTP request. The request may pass through a CDN, load balancer and reverse proxy before reaching the application server, which queries databases or caches, builds a response, and returns it. The browser then renders HTML and fetches further assets.
keyPoints: Mention DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP, load balancing, caching, application and database
Name where failures show up: DNS errors, timeouts, certificate errors, 5xx codes
A good answer adds CDN, keep-alive connections and HTTP/2 or HTTP/3
Debug with dig, curl -v and browser dev tools

concepts.name: Q: How do you troubleshoot a server with high load average?
concepts.explanation: I first compare load to the number of CPU cores with uptime, then use top or htop to see whether CPU, memory or IO is the cause. vmstat shows run queue, swapping and IO wait, iostat shows disk latency and utilisation, and pidstat or ps identifies the process. High load with low CPU usually means processes are blocked on disk or network IO. After finding the culprit I check logs, recent deployments and cron jobs, then fix, scale, or limit it.
keyPoints: Load average counts runnable and uninterruptible processes, not just CPU use
Tools: uptime, top, vmstat, iostat, free, ss, dmesg, strace, perf
Check dmesg for OOM kills and disk errors
Add alerting on saturation metrics so you catch it earlier

concepts.name: Q: Explain Linux file permissions (chmod 755, 644, setuid).
concepts.explanation: Every file has read, write and execute permissions for the owner, the group and everyone else. Permissions are written in octal: read is 4, write is 2, execute is 1, so 755 means owner can read, write and execute while group and others can read and execute; 644 means the owner can read and write and everyone else can only read. setuid makes an executable run with the owner's privileges, setgid does the same for the group (and makes new files inherit the directory group), and the sticky bit on a directory stops users deleting each other's files.
keyPoints: Use chmod, chown and chgrp; check with ls -l and namei -l
Avoid 777; fix ownership or group membership instead
Directories need execute permission to be entered
umask defines default permissions for new files

concepts.name: Q: What is the difference between a process and a thread, and what is a zombie process?
concepts.explanation: A process is an independent program instance with its own memory space, while threads are lightweight execution units inside a process that share its memory. Threads are cheaper to create and communicate faster but can corrupt shared state without synchronisation. A zombie is a finished child process whose exit status has not yet been read by its parent; it uses no resources except a process table entry and is removed once the parent calls wait or exits.
keyPoints: Signals: SIGTERM (graceful), SIGKILL (cannot be caught), SIGHUP (reload)
In containers the first process is PID 1 and must reap children and handle signals (use tini or --init)
ps shows zombies in state Z
Fix zombies by fixing or restarting the parent process

concepts.name: Q: What is the difference between a hard link and a symbolic link?
concepts.explanation: A hard link is another directory entry pointing to the same inode, so both names refer to identical data and the data survives until all links are removed; it cannot cross filesystems or link directories. A symbolic link is a small file containing a path to another file; it can cross filesystems and point to directories, but it breaks if the target is moved or removed.
keyPoints: ln file hard (hard link), ln -s target link (symbolic link)
Hard links share the inode number (ls -i)
Deleting the original does not affect a hard link but dangles a symlink
Symlinks are common in deployment layouts (current -> releases/42)

concepts.name: Q: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
concepts.explanation: TCP is connection-oriented and reliable: it establishes a connection with a handshake, guarantees ordered delivery with acknowledgements and retransmission, and applies flow and congestion control. UDP is connectionless and sends independent datagrams without delivery guarantees, so it is faster with lower overhead. TCP suits web, SSH and databases; UDP suits DNS, streaming, gaming and QUIC.
keyPoints: TCP three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK
HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP to avoid head-of-line blocking
Load balancers can operate on either (L4 NLB)
Use nc -u for UDP tests

concepts.name: Q: How does DNS work, and what are the common record types?
concepts.explanation: When a client needs an IP, it asks a recursive resolver, which checks its cache and otherwise queries the root servers, then the top-level domain servers, then the domain's authoritative servers, caching the answer according to its TTL. Common records are A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias to another name), MX (mail), TXT (verification, SPF), NS (name servers) and SRV. DNS issues are a frequent cause of outages, so I check it early with dig.
keyPoints: Lower TTLs before a migration; propagation is really cache expiry
CNAME cannot sit at the zone apex; use ALIAS/ANAME records
Tools: dig, nslookup, host; dig +trace shows the full chain
Inside Kubernetes, CoreDNS resolves service names

concepts.name: Q: What is the difference between a security group and a network ACL?
concepts.explanation: A security group is a stateful firewall attached to an instance or network interface that only has allow rules; return traffic for an allowed connection is permitted automatically. A network ACL is a stateless firewall attached to a subnet with ordered allow and deny rules, so you must allow return traffic explicitly. Security groups are the main tool; NACLs add subnet-level guardrails or explicit denies.
keyPoints: Security groups can reference other security groups instead of IP ranges
NACL rules are evaluated in number order, first match wins
Both are default-deny for inbound unless rules exist (default NACL allows all)
Combine with OS firewalls and Kubernetes NetworkPolicies for depth

concepts.name: Q: Explain subnetting and CIDR. How many IPs are in a /24?
concepts.explanation: CIDR notation writes an address with a prefix length that says how many leading bits identify the network. A /24 leaves 8 bits for hosts, so it contains 256 addresses (254 usable on a traditional network; cloud providers reserve a few more). A /16 contains 65,536 addresses. Subnets divide a larger network into smaller segments for isolation, routing and security, such as separate public, private and database subnets.
keyPoints: Plan non-overlapping CIDR ranges to allow VPC peering and VPN
Each additional prefix bit halves the number of addresses
Public subnet routes to an internet gateway; private subnet uses NAT

concepts.name: Q: A service is running but you cannot connect to it. How do you debug?
concepts.explanation: I work from the server outward. Confirm the process is listening on the expected address and port with ss -tulpn, remembering that 127.0.0.1 is only local. Test locally with curl, then from another host with nc -zv or curl. If it fails remotely, check the host firewall, cloud security group, network ACL and route tables, then the load balancer health checks and DNS. Logs on the app and proxy confirm whether requests arrive at all.
keyPoints: Connection refused = nothing listening; timeout = packets dropped by a firewall or route
Bind to 0.0.0.0 (or the correct interface), not just localhost
tcpdump verifies whether packets actually reach the host
In Kubernetes: check Pod, Service endpoints, DNS, NetworkPolicy and Ingress in that order

concepts.name: Q: What is the difference between cron and systemd timers?
concepts.explanation: Cron runs commands on a schedule defined by a five-field expression and is simple and universal. systemd timers pair with service units, so they get dependency handling, logging in journald, resource controls, randomised delays, and can catch up missed runs after downtime (Persistent=true). For new Linux-only automation timers are more powerful, while cron remains common for quick jobs.
keyPoints: Cron has a minimal environment: use absolute paths and redirect output
Use flock to prevent overlapping runs of the same job
In Kubernetes use CronJob; in the cloud use EventBridge Scheduler or similar
Always monitor scheduled jobs so silent failures are detected

concepts.name: Q: How would you find which process is using a port, or filling the disk?
concepts.explanation: For ports I use ss -tulpn or lsof -i :PORT to show the listening process and PID. For disk space I start with df -h to find the full filesystem and df -i for inodes, then du -xh --max-depth=1 repeatedly (or ncdu) to drill into the largest directories. If space seems used but files are missing, lsof +L1 reveals deleted files still held open by a running process, which a restart releases.
keyPoints: Typical culprits: logs, Docker images and volumes, core dumps, package caches
Configure logrotate and Docker log limits
Full inodes also cause "No space left on device"
Alert at 80% disk usage, not at 100%

concepts.name: Q: Write a shell one-liner to find the top 10 IP addresses in an access log.
concepts.explanation: Extract the IP column, sort it so identical lines are adjacent, count each unique value, sort numerically in descending order, and take the first ten. This is the classic sort and uniq counting idiom.
concepts.code:
awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -10

# Variations
awk '$9 >= 500 {print $7}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head   # top failing URLs
grep "POST /login" access.log | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head   # brute-force suspects
keyPoints: uniq only collapses adjacent duplicates, which is why sort comes first
awk columns depend on the log format; check a sample line first
For huge logs use zcat for rotated files or a log platform query
Mention jq for JSON logs

concepts.name: Q: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?
concepts.explanation: Merge combines two branches by creating a merge commit that keeps the true history of both lines of work. Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch, creating new commits and a linear history. Rebase gives a cleaner history but rewrites commits, so it should only be used on local or private branches, never on shared history. Merge is safer for shared branches; many teams use squash merge for pull requests.
keyPoints: Never rebase commits that others have pulled
git pull --rebase keeps local history linear
Resolve conflicts once per commit when rebasing, once when merging
Interactive rebase (git rebase -i) tidies commits before opening a PR

concepts.name: Q: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull, and git reset vs git revert?
concepts.explanation: git fetch downloads new commits from the remote without changing your working branch; git pull is fetch plus merge (or rebase). git reset moves the branch pointer (and optionally the index and working tree) to an earlier commit, rewriting history, which is fine locally. git revert creates a new commit that undoes a previous commit, preserving history, which is the safe way to undo changes that are already pushed.
keyPoints: Use revert on shared branches such as main
reset --soft keeps changes staged, --mixed unstages them, --hard discards them
git reflog can recover commits after an accidental reset
git restore and git switch are the modern, clearer commands for files and branches

concepts.name: Q: Which branching strategy would you recommend and why?
concepts.explanation: For most teams practising CI/CD I recommend trunk-based development: short-lived branches merged into main at least daily, protected by required reviews and checks, with feature flags to hide unfinished work. It minimises merge pain and keeps the main branch releasable. GitFlow with long-lived develop and release branches suits scheduled, versioned releases such as mobile apps, but it slows integration and adds overhead.
keyPoints: Pair with small PRs, fast CI and automated deploys
Protect main: no direct pushes, required status checks
Environment branches cause drift; promote artifacts instead
Choose according to release cadence, team size and product type

concepts.name: Q: How would you design a CI/CD pipeline for a microservices application?
concepts.explanation: Each service has its own repository or path-filtered pipeline that runs on every pull request: lint, unit tests, static analysis and dependency scan, then builds a container image tagged with the git SHA, scans it and pushes it to a registry. On merge, CD deploys automatically to a dev environment, runs integration and smoke tests, promotes the same image to staging and then production using a rolling or canary strategy, and rolls back on failed health or SLO checks. Infrastructure is managed with Terraform and deployments use GitOps with Argo CD. Contract tests keep services independently deployable, and metrics feed back into the pipeline.
keyPoints: Build once, promote the same artifact; keep config outside the image
Parallelise independent jobs and cache dependencies
Secrets via OIDC and a secret manager; sign images
Observe deployments: tag releases in dashboards and alert on regressions

concepts.name: Q: How do you make a pipeline faster and more reliable?
concepts.explanation: For speed I parallelise independent jobs, cache dependencies and Docker layers, use path filters to run only affected services, split slow tests into shards, use bigger or self-hosted runners where it pays, and run quick checks first so failures surface early. For reliability I make jobs idempotent and deterministic with pinned versions and lockfiles, quarantine flaky tests, use ephemeral runners, add timeouts and retries only for genuinely transient steps, and monitor pipeline duration and failure rate over time.
keyPoints: Target under ten minutes for PR feedback
Fail fast: lint and unit tests before integration
Treat flaky tests as bugs with an owner
Keep pipeline logic in scripts so it is runnable locally

concepts.name: Q: Explain blue/green, canary and rolling deployments.
concepts.explanation: In a rolling deployment instances are replaced gradually with the new version, with no extra environment but a slower rollback. Blue/green runs the new version in a parallel environment, tests it, then switches all traffic at once, allowing instant rollback at the cost of double capacity. Canary sends a small share of real traffic to the new version, increases it while watching metrics, and aborts automatically if errors rise, giving the smallest blast radius but requiring good observability and traffic splitting.
keyPoints: Kubernetes default is rolling; Argo Rollouts or Flagger add canary and blue/green
All three need backward-compatible database changes
Feature flags decouple deployment from release
Pick based on risk, cost and the ability to measure health

concepts.name: Q: How do you handle database changes in continuous deployment?
concepts.explanation: I treat schema changes as versioned migrations stored in Git and applied by a tool such as Flyway or Liquibase in a controlled pipeline step. To avoid downtime and allow rollback of the application I use the expand and contract pattern: add new columns or tables in a backward-compatible way, deploy code that works with both schemas, migrate data, and only remove old structures in a later release. I test migrations on production-like data and take backups before risky changes.
keyPoints: Never drop or rename a column in the same release that stops using it
Run migrations once as a Job or pipeline step, not on every app replica start
Large backfills run in batches outside the deploy path
Rolling forward with a fix is often safer than reverting a schema

concepts.name: Q: How do you secure a CI/CD pipeline?
concepts.explanation: I use least-privilege, short-lived credentials (OIDC to the cloud instead of stored keys), keep secrets in a manager and mask them in logs, pin actions and dependencies to immutable versions or hashes, and run builds on ephemeral isolated runners. Branch protection and required reviews guard the pipeline files themselves. I add scanning for secrets, dependencies, images and IaC, sign artifacts, and avoid running untrusted pull-request code with access to secrets.
keyPoints: Dangerous patterns: pull_request_target with fork code, long-lived tokens, shared persistent runners
Separate build credentials from deploy credentials
Use protected environments with approvals for production
Audit pipeline changes like production code

concepts.name: Q: What is GitOps and how is it different from traditional CI/CD pushing to a cluster?
concepts.explanation: GitOps keeps the desired state of the system declaratively in Git, and an agent in the cluster such as Argo CD or Flux continuously pulls that state and reconciles the cluster to match it. In a traditional push model the CI system holds cluster credentials and runs kubectl or helm. GitOps improves security because the cluster pulls changes, gives a full audit trail and easy rollback by reverting a commit, and corrects drift automatically.
keyPoints: CI builds and updates the image tag in the config repo; the agent deploys
Separate application and configuration repositories
Secrets need encryption (SOPS, Sealed Secrets) or an external secrets operator
Rollback is a git revert, not a manual kubectl command

concepts.name: Q: How do you version and tag releases and container images?
concepts.explanation: I use semantic versioning for releases, generated from conventional commits, and tag the git commit with the version. Container images get an immutable tag with the commit SHA that is deployed, plus convenient release tags like 1.4.2 and 1.4. I avoid depending on latest, and for critical deployments I reference the image digest. The same image is promoted across environments without rebuilding.
keyPoints: Tools: semantic-release, release-please, docker/metadata-action
Embed version and commit in the app (build args or labels) for traceability
Immutable tags and registry lifecycle policies prevent surprises and runaway storage
Always be able to answer "which commit is running in production?"

concepts.name: Q: A deployment succeeded in the pipeline but users report errors. What do you do?
concepts.explanation: First I check the deployment time against the start of errors, then look at dashboards for error rate and latency by version. If the new release correlates with the problem I roll back or disable the feature flag immediately to restore service, then investigate. I compare logs and traces from before and after, check configuration and dependency changes, confirm which image digest is really running, and finally add a test, canary analysis or alert so the pipeline catches it next time.
keyPoints: Mitigation first, root cause second
Verify the running version: kubectl get pod -o jsonpath for the imageID
Deployment markers in Grafana make correlation easy
Add post-deploy smoke tests and automated rollback

concepts.name: Q: What is the difference between a container and a virtual machine?
concepts.explanation: A virtual machine emulates hardware and runs a complete guest operating system on a hypervisor, giving strong isolation but heavy resource use and slow startup. A container packages an application with its dependencies and runs as an isolated process on the host kernel using namespaces and cgroups, so it is lightweight and starts in seconds. Containers share the kernel, so isolation is weaker than a VM, and a container can only run workloads compatible with the host kernel.
keyPoints: VMs: GBs, minutes; containers: MBs, seconds
Namespaces isolate what a process sees; cgroups limit what it can use
Many systems combine them: containers running inside VMs
Sandboxed runtimes (gVisor, Kata Containers) increase container isolation

concepts.name: Q: What is the difference between an image and a container, and what are layers?
concepts.explanation: An image is a read-only template built from instructions, made of stacked layers; a container is a running instance of an image with a thin writable layer on top. Each Dockerfile instruction that changes the filesystem creates a layer that is cached and shared between images, which makes builds and pulls efficient. Changes inside a running container are lost when it is removed unless stored in a volume.
keyPoints: Order instructions from least to most frequently changing to maximise cache hits
docker history shows layers; smaller and fewer layers help pull times
Union filesystems such as overlay2 present layers as a single filesystem
One image can start many containers

concepts.name: Q: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT, and COPY vs ADD?
concepts.explanation: ENTRYPOINT defines the executable that always runs, while CMD supplies default arguments (or the default command when no ENTRYPOINT exists) that can be overridden at docker run. They are often combined: ENTRYPOINT is the program and CMD is its default arguments. COPY simply copies files from the build context; ADD additionally extracts local tar archives and can download URLs, which makes it less predictable, so COPY is preferred.
keyPoints: Use exec form (JSON array) so the process is PID 1 and receives signals
Shell form wraps the command in sh -c and can swallow SIGTERM
RUN executes at build time; CMD/ENTRYPOINT at container start
ARG is build-time only; ENV persists into the running container

concepts.name: Q: How do you reduce Docker image size and improve security?
concepts.explanation: Use a small, specific base image (slim, alpine or distroless), build with multi-stage builds so compilers and build tools stay out of the final image, copy only needed files, combine and clean package-manager steps in one layer, and maintain a .dockerignore. For security run as a non-root user, pin base versions, avoid secrets in layers, scan images with Trivy, keep images patched, drop capabilities and use a read-only root filesystem where possible.
keyPoints: Multi-stage builds usually give the largest size reduction
Distroless images have no shell or package manager, reducing attack surface
Sign images and generate SBOMs
Check docker history and tools like dive to find bloat

concepts.name: Q: How do Docker networking and volumes work?
concepts.explanation: Containers on a user-defined bridge network get their own IPs and can reach each other by container name through Docker's embedded DNS, while published ports (-p) expose services on the host. Other drivers include host (shares the host stack), none, overlay (multi-host) and macvlan. Because container filesystems are ephemeral, persistent data goes into named volumes managed by Docker or bind mounts of host paths; tmpfs mounts keep data in memory only.
keyPoints: Prefer user-defined networks over the default bridge
Volumes survive container removal and are the right choice for databases
Bind mounts are convenient in development but tie containers to the host layout
In Kubernetes the equivalents are Services, PersistentVolumeClaims and emptyDir

concepts.name: Q: A container keeps restarting or exits immediately. How do you debug it?
concepts.explanation: I check docker ps -a for the status and exit code, read the logs with docker logs, and inspect the configuration with docker inspect. Exit code 137 suggests SIGKILL or out-of-memory, 143 SIGTERM, 1 an application error, and 127 a missing command. I try running the image interactively with a shell override (docker run -it --entrypoint sh image) to inspect files and environment. Common causes are missing environment variables, wrong command, permission errors, failing dependencies and health checks.
keyPoints: A container exits when its main process ends; make sure it runs in the foreground
docker events and docker stats help with resource problems
Compare environment and mounted files with a working setup
On Kubernetes use kubectl logs --previous and describe pod

concepts.name: Q: How do containers isolate resources? What are namespaces and cgroups?
concepts.explanation: Linux namespaces give a container its own view of system resources: process IDs, network interfaces, mount points, hostname, users and inter-process communication. Control groups (cgroups) limit and account for the resources a group of processes may consume — CPU, memory, disk IO and process count. Together with a layered filesystem and security features such as seccomp, capabilities and AppArmor or SELinux, they form the container sandbox.
keyPoints: Memory limit exceeded leads to the OOM killer; CPU limit exceeded leads to throttling
Root inside a container is not necessarily root on the host, especially with user namespaces
Rootless Docker and Podman reduce risk further
Kernel exploits can still escape, which is why VMs or sandboxes are used for untrusted code

concepts.name: Q: What is the difference between Docker Compose and Kubernetes?
concepts.explanation: Docker Compose defines and runs multi-container applications on a single host, ideal for local development and small deployments. Kubernetes orchestrates containers across a cluster of machines, adding scheduling, self-healing, rolling updates, autoscaling, service discovery, secrets and storage abstractions, and is designed for production at scale. Compose is simple and quick to learn; Kubernetes is far more powerful but operationally heavier.
keyPoints: Compose files can be converted or used as a design starting point
Docker Swarm is Docker's simpler built-in orchestrator, now rarely chosen for new projects
Managed container services (ECS, Cloud Run) sit between the two in complexity
Choose Kubernetes only when you need its features

concepts.name: Q: How would you handle persistent data and logging for containers?
concepts.explanation: Containers should be stateless: persistent data goes to external managed databases or to volumes mounted from durable storage, and application logs go to stdout and stderr so the platform collects them. A log driver or agent such as Fluent Bit ships logs to a central system like Loki, Elasticsearch or CloudWatch. I configure log rotation limits on the Docker daemon to avoid filling the disk.
keyPoints: Twelve-factor: treat logs as event streams
Back up volumes and test restores
Avoid writing logs to files inside the container
Use structured JSON logs with request IDs

concepts.name: Q: What is the difference between docker stop and docker kill, and how does graceful shutdown work?
concepts.explanation: docker stop sends SIGTERM to the main process, waits for a grace period (10 seconds by default), and then sends SIGKILL; docker kill sends SIGKILL immediately (or a chosen signal). For graceful shutdown the application must handle SIGTERM by finishing in-flight requests, closing connections and exiting, and it must be PID 1 or be started through an init process that forwards signals. Kubernetes follows the same sequence with terminationGracePeriodSeconds and preStop hooks.
keyPoints: Shell-form commands often prevent signal delivery; use exec form
Use docker run --init or tini to reap zombies and forward signals
Match the grace period to your longest request or drain time
Without graceful handling, rolling deploys drop requests

concepts.name: Q: Explain Kubernetes architecture.
concepts.explanation: Kubernetes has a control plane and worker nodes. The control plane consists of the API server (the single entry point), etcd (the key-value store holding all cluster state), the scheduler (assigns Pods to nodes), and the controller manager (runs controllers that reconcile desired and actual state), plus the cloud controller manager. Each worker node runs the kubelet (starts and monitors Pods), kube-proxy (implements Service networking) and a container runtime such as containerd. Users declare desired state through the API and controllers continuously make reality match it.
keyPoints: Only the API server reads and writes etcd; back up etcd
Managed services (EKS, GKE, AKS) operate the control plane for you
Flow: kubectl apply, API server stores in etcd, scheduler picks a node, kubelet runs the Pod
Add-ons: CoreDNS, CNI plugin, metrics-server, ingress/gateway controller

concepts.name: Q: What happens when you run kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml?
concepts.explanation: kubectl sends the manifest to the API server, which authenticates, authorises and validates it, runs admission controllers, and stores the Deployment object in etcd. The Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet, which creates Pod objects. The scheduler assigns each unscheduled Pod to a suitable node, the kubelet on that node pulls the image and starts the containers through the runtime, and probes decide when the Pod becomes ready and receives Service traffic.
keyPoints: Everything is event-driven and goes through the API server
Controllers run reconciliation loops: observe, compare, act
Admission controllers can mutate or reject requests (policy, defaults)
You can watch the sequence with kubectl get events

concepts.name: Q: What is the difference between a Deployment, ReplicaSet, StatefulSet and DaemonSet?
concepts.explanation: A ReplicaSet keeps a specified number of identical Pods running. A Deployment manages ReplicaSets to provide declarative rolling updates and rollbacks for stateless apps. A StatefulSet gives Pods stable names, ordered startup and per-Pod persistent storage, for databases and clustered systems. A DaemonSet ensures one Pod runs on every (or selected) node, used for log collectors, monitoring agents and network plugins.
keyPoints: You rarely create ReplicaSets directly
Jobs and CronJobs run Pods to completion or on a schedule
StatefulSets need a headless Service for stable DNS names
Prefer managed databases to running stateful systems yourself

concepts.name: Q: How do Kubernetes Services work, and what are the Service types?
concepts.explanation: A Service gives a set of Pods, selected by labels, a stable virtual IP and DNS name and load-balances traffic across the ready Pods; kube-proxy programs iptables or IPVS rules to implement it. ClusterIP is internal only, NodePort opens a port on every node, LoadBalancer provisions a cloud load balancer, and ExternalName maps to an external DNS name. A headless Service (clusterIP: None) returns the Pod IPs directly, used with StatefulSets.
keyPoints: Pods are ephemeral; clients must use the Service, not Pod IPs
Endpoints/EndpointSlices list the ready Pod addresses
Ingress or Gateway API provides HTTP routing in front of Services
No endpoints usually means a selector/label mismatch or failing readiness probes

concepts.name: Q: What is the difference between liveness, readiness and startup probes?
concepts.explanation: The liveness probe checks whether a container is still healthy; if it fails, the kubelet restarts the container. The readiness probe checks whether it can serve traffic; if it fails, the Pod is removed from Service endpoints without a restart. The startup probe gives slow-starting applications extra time and disables the other probes until it succeeds. Misconfigured probes are a frequent cause of cascading restarts.
keyPoints: Liveness should not check dependencies such as the database, or a DB outage restarts every Pod
Readiness can check dependencies and warm-up status
Tune initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds and failureThreshold to the app's real behaviour
Combine with preStop and graceful shutdown for zero-downtime deploys

concepts.name: Q: What are requests and limits, and what happens when they are exceeded?
concepts.explanation: Requests are the resources the scheduler reserves for a container and the basis for placement and Pod QoS; limits are the maximum it may use. If a container exceeds its CPU limit it is throttled, but if it exceeds its memory limit it is OOMKilled (exit code 137). Pods with requests equal to limits are Guaranteed QoS and are evicted last under node pressure, Burstable have some requests, and BestEffort have none and are evicted first.
keyPoints: Set memory request equal to limit; be careful with strict CPU limits because throttling hurts latency
ResourceQuota and LimitRange enforce defaults and ceilings per namespace
HPA calculates utilisation relative to requests
Right-size using metrics or Vertical Pod Autoscaler recommendations

concepts.name: Q: A Pod is stuck in Pending, CrashLoopBackOff or ImagePullBackOff. What do you check?
concepts.explanation: I always start with kubectl describe pod and read the Events. Pending usually means the scheduler cannot place it because of insufficient resources, taints, node selectors, or an unbound PVC. ImagePullBackOff means a wrong image name or tag, missing registry credentials or rate limiting. CrashLoopBackOff means the container starts and exits repeatedly, so I read kubectl logs --previous for the cause — typically bad configuration, missing environment or secrets, an application bug, an OOM kill or a failing liveness probe.
keyPoints: Exit code 137 = SIGKILL/OOM; 1 = app error; 127 = command not found
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp shows recent cluster events
kubectl debug creates an ephemeral container for shell-less images
Fix the cause rather than raising restart limits

concepts.name: Q: How do you do zero-downtime deployments in Kubernetes?
concepts.explanation: Use a Deployment with a RollingUpdate strategy (maxUnavailable 0, maxSurge 1 or a percentage) so new Pods become ready before old ones are removed. Correct readiness probes keep traffic away from Pods that are not ready, and a preStop hook plus handling SIGTERM and a sufficient terminationGracePeriodSeconds let in-flight requests finish. Multiple replicas, a PodDisruptionBudget and topology spread keep capacity during updates and node drains.
keyPoints: Backward-compatible database changes are essential
For finer control use canary or blue/green with Argo Rollouts, Flagger or Gateway API weights
kubectl rollout status gates the pipeline; rollout undo reverts
Test the procedure under load, not just on an idle cluster

concepts.name: Q: What is the difference between ConfigMap and Secret? Are Secrets secure?
concepts.explanation: ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive configuration and Secrets hold sensitive data such as passwords and tokens; both can be exposed as environment variables or mounted files. By default Secrets are only base64-encoded and stored unencrypted in etcd, so they are not secure by themselves. To protect them enable encryption at rest, restrict access with RBAC, avoid exposing them via environment variables where possible, and ideally source them from an external secret manager through External Secrets Operator or the CSI driver.
keyPoints: Mounted values update eventually; environment variables need a Pod restart
Anyone who can create a Pod in a namespace can read its Secrets
Sealed Secrets and SOPS allow encrypted secrets in Git
Use workload identity instead of static cloud credentials

concepts.name: Q: Explain Ingress vs Service vs Gateway API, and what is an Ingress controller?
concepts.explanation: A Service provides internal load balancing (or a cloud load balancer) at layer 4. An Ingress defines HTTP and HTTPS routing rules by host and path to Services, and needs an Ingress controller — a running component such as Traefik, HAProxy or a cloud controller — to implement the rules. Gateway API is the newer, more expressive and role-oriented standard with GatewayClass, Gateway and HTTPRoute resources, supporting traffic splitting and more protocols. The widely used community ingress-nginx project was retired in March 2026, so new designs should pick a maintained controller or Gateway API.
keyPoints: One Ingress/Gateway can front many Services, avoiding one cloud load balancer per Service
cert-manager automates TLS certificates
Annotations are controller-specific; Gateway API reduces that
ingress2gateway helps migrate existing Ingress resources

concepts.name: Q: How does autoscaling work in Kubernetes?
concepts.explanation: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adjusts the replica count of a Deployment based on metrics such as CPU utilisation, memory or custom metrics. The Vertical Pod Autoscaler recommends or sets container requests, and the Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter adds and removes nodes when Pods cannot be scheduled or nodes are underused. KEDA adds event-driven scaling, including to zero. They work together: HPA creates more Pods, then node autoscaling provides the capacity.
keyPoints: HPA needs metrics-server and resource requests
Add a PodDisruptionBudget and sensible scale-down stabilisation to prevent flapping
Scale on the metric that reflects load, such as requests per second or queue length
Do not let HPA and VPA both act on CPU for the same workload

concepts.name: Q: What is RBAC in Kubernetes and how do you apply least privilege?
concepts.explanation: Role-Based Access Control authorises API requests using Roles (namespaced) or ClusterRoles that list allowed verbs on resources, attached to users, groups or ServiceAccounts by RoleBindings or ClusterRoleBindings. For least privilege I grant narrowly scoped Roles instead of cluster-admin, give each workload its own ServiceAccount with only the permissions it needs, disable automatic token mounting where unnecessary, and audit with kubectl auth can-i and tools like rbac-lookup.
keyPoints: Treat permission to read Secrets or exec into Pods as highly privileged
Use cloud workload identity (IRSA, Workload Identity) for cloud API access
Review RBAC regularly; avoid wildcard verbs and resources
Combine with Pod Security Admission and NetworkPolicies

concepts.name: Q: How do you troubleshoot a Service that is not reachable?
concepts.explanation: I trace the path layer by layer. Check Pods are Running and Ready, then check the Service selector matches the Pod labels and that kubectl get endpoints shows addresses. Test from inside the cluster with a debug Pod (curl the Service name, nslookup for DNS), verify targetPort matches the container port, and rule out NetworkPolicies. For external access check the Ingress or Gateway, the controller logs, the cloud load balancer health and security groups, and the DNS record.
keyPoints: Empty endpoints = selector or readiness problem
kubectl port-forward isolates whether the app itself works
CoreDNS logs help with name-resolution issues
502/503 from ingress means no healthy backend; 504 means timeout

concepts.name: Q: What are taints, tolerations, node affinity and Pod disruption budgets?
concepts.explanation: Taints on nodes repel Pods unless they have a matching toleration, used to reserve nodes for special workloads like GPUs. Node affinity and nodeSelector attract Pods to nodes with certain labels, while pod affinity and anti-affinity place Pods near or away from other Pods, for example spreading replicas across nodes. A PodDisruptionBudget limits how many replicas can be voluntarily evicted at once, protecting availability during node drains and upgrades.
keyPoints: Tolerations permit scheduling but do not force it; combine with affinity
topologySpreadConstraints spread Pods evenly across zones
kubectl drain respects PDBs; cordon marks a node unschedulable
Priority classes decide who is preempted under pressure

concepts.name: Q: How do you upgrade a Kubernetes cluster safely?
concepts.explanation: Read the release notes and deprecated APIs, check that add-ons and workloads support the target version, and upgrade one minor version at a time. Back up etcd and test in a non-production cluster first. Upgrade the control plane, then node pools gradually using surge or rolling replacement, draining nodes while PodDisruptionBudgets protect availability, and monitor throughout. Managed services automate much of this, but you still validate workloads and API deprecations.
keyPoints: Tools: pluto and kubent detect removed APIs; kubeadm upgrade for self-managed clusters
Version skew policy: kubelet may lag the API server by a limited number of minor versions
Blue/green cluster upgrades are an alternative for high-risk changes
Supported minor versions get roughly a year of patches, so plan upgrades regularly

concepts.name: Q: What is Helm and how does it differ from Kustomize?
concepts.explanation: Helm is a package manager that bundles Kubernetes manifests into charts with Go templates and a values file, supports versioned releases, upgrades and rollbacks, and distributes software through repositories or OCI registries. Kustomize applies declarative overlays and patches on plain YAML without templating, which is simple and built into kubectl. Helm suits packaging and third-party software; Kustomize suits environment-specific variations of your own manifests, and the two are often combined.
keyPoints: helm template and helm diff show what would be applied
helm upgrade --install is the idempotent CI/CD command
Helm 4 renamed --atomic to --rollback-on-failure and --force to --force-replace
Keep charts simple and values documented

concepts.name: Q: Explain the Terraform workflow and what the state file is.
concepts.explanation: The workflow is write configuration, terraform init to download providers and configure the backend, terraform plan to preview the diff between code, state and real infrastructure, and terraform apply to make the changes. The state file maps resources in the code to real objects and stores their attributes, so Terraform knows what to create, update or destroy. State should live in a remote backend with locking and encryption, because it can contain secrets and concurrent writes can corrupt it.
keyPoints: Never edit state manually; use terraform state mv/rm and import
Remote backends: S3 (with native locking), GCS, Azure Blob, Terraform Cloud
State per environment and component limits blast radius
Save the plan and apply that exact plan in CI

concepts.name: Q: What happens if two people run terraform apply at the same time?
concepts.explanation: Without locking they could both read the same state and overwrite each other's changes, corrupting the state or creating duplicate resources. Remote backends solve this with state locking: the first run acquires a lock and the second fails with a message saying the state is locked. The S3 backend now supports native locking with use_lockfile, which replaces the older DynamoDB table approach. If a run crashes and leaves a stale lock, terraform force-unlock releases it after you confirm nobody is applying.
keyPoints: Run Terraform only from CI to serialise changes
Use separate state files for independent stacks
Atlantis, Terraform Cloud or Spacelift queue and lock runs for you
Never force-unlock while another apply may still be running

concepts.name: Q: How do you handle drift and import existing infrastructure?
concepts.explanation: For drift I run terraform plan (or plan -refresh-only) on a schedule to detect differences between state and reality, then either update the code to match a legitimate change or apply to revert an unauthorised one, and restrict console access to prevent recurrence. To bring existing resources under management I write the matching configuration and use terraform import or import blocks, then run plan until it shows no changes.
keyPoints: terraform state list/show helps inspect what is tracked
moved blocks refactor resource addresses without recreating resources
lifecycle ignore_changes tolerates attributes managed elsewhere
Tools like Terraformer or cloud export features can generate starting code

concepts.name: Q: What is the difference between count and for_each, and when do you use modules?
concepts.explanation: count creates a number of instances indexed by position, so removing an item from the middle shifts the indexes and may recreate resources. for_each iterates over a map or set and keys each instance by name, so adding or removing one item only affects that one, and it is generally preferred. Modules package reusable infrastructure patterns with inputs and outputs, so you can create the same VPC or cluster for many environments without copying code.
keyPoints: count is fine for simple on/off toggles (count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0)
Pin module versions; keep modules small and documented
dynamic blocks generate repeated nested blocks
Use depends_on only when implicit references are not enough

concepts.name: Q: How do you manage secrets and multiple environments in Terraform?
concepts.explanation: Never hard-code secrets in code or variables files committed to Git. I read them from a secret manager through data sources or inject them at runtime from the pipeline, mark variables as sensitive, and remember that values still appear in state, so the state backend must be encrypted and access-controlled. For environments I use separate directories or workspaces with separate state and backend per environment, shared modules for the common code, and different variable files, with promotion through pull requests.
keyPoints: Prefer ephemeral values and write-only attributes where the provider supports them
Use OIDC roles for pipeline credentials
Separate accounts or projects per environment
Terragrunt reduces repetition across many environments

concepts.name: Q: Terraform vs Ansible vs CloudFormation vs Pulumi?
concepts.explanation: Terraform is a declarative, multi-cloud provisioning tool using HCL and a state file. Ansible is an agentless configuration management and orchestration tool using YAML playbooks over SSH, best for configuring servers and one-off tasks. CloudFormation is AWS-native declarative provisioning with state managed by AWS, and CDK generates it from code. Pulumi provisions infrastructure with general-purpose programming languages. A common split is Terraform to create infrastructure and Ansible to configure what runs on it, though containers reduce the need for the latter.
keyPoints: Declarative: you describe the end state; procedural: you describe steps
OpenTofu is the open-source fork of Terraform
Provisioning vs configuration management is the core distinction
Choose by multi-cloud needs, team language skills and ecosystem

concepts.name: Q: What is idempotency in Ansible, and what are handlers, roles and Vault?
concepts.explanation: Idempotency means running a playbook repeatedly produces the same end state and only changes what is needed, because modules check current state before acting; raw shell commands break this unless guarded. Handlers are tasks that run only when notified by a change, typically to restart or reload a service after its configuration file changed. Roles package tasks, templates, defaults and handlers into reusable units, and Ansible Vault encrypts sensitive variables so they can be stored in version control.
keyPoints: Use modules (apt, service, template) instead of command or shell
--check and --diff preview changes
Variable precedence is a common gotcha
Test roles with Molecule and lint with ansible-lint

concepts.name: Q: How would you provision a highly available web application on AWS with Terraform?
concepts.explanation: I would define a VPC with public and private subnets across at least two availability zones, an Application Load Balancer in the public subnets, and an Auto Scaling Group or EKS node group in the private subnets reaching the internet through NAT gateways. The data layer is RDS Multi-AZ in isolated subnets, with security groups allowing only the necessary flows, and IAM roles instead of keys. Remote state with locking, modules per component, CloudWatch alarms, and a pipeline that runs plan on pull requests and apply on merge complete the setup.
keyPoints: State the failure domains you protect against (instance, AZ)
Add WAF and CloudFront for edge protection and caching
Use Secrets Manager and KMS for secrets and encryption
Mention cost trade-offs, for example one NAT per AZ versus one shared NAT

concepts.name: Q: What is the shared responsibility model?
concepts.explanation: The cloud provider is responsible for security of the cloud — physical data centres, hardware, networking and the virtualisation layer — while the customer is responsible for security in the cloud: identity and access management, data, application code, network configuration and operating-system patching where applicable. The more managed the service, the more the provider takes on, but data and access control always remain the customer's job.
keyPoints: IaaS: you manage OS and above; PaaS: you manage app and data; SaaS: mostly configuration and access
Most breaches come from customer misconfiguration such as public buckets
Use tools like Security Hub, Config and Access Analyzer to detect issues
Compliance certifications of the provider do not make your workload compliant automatically

concepts.name: Q: Explain IAM users, groups, roles and policies. Why prefer roles?
concepts.explanation: IAM identities are users (long-term credentials for a person or app), groups (collections of users), and roles (identities that are assumed temporarily and get short-lived credentials). Policies are JSON documents granting or denying actions on resources and are attached to identities or resources. Roles are preferred because there are no long-lived secrets to leak or rotate: EC2 instances, Lambda functions, ECS tasks, EKS ServiceAccounts and CI pipelines assume roles automatically.
keyPoints: Explicit deny overrides allow; default is deny
Use SSO (IAM Identity Center) for humans and MFA everywhere
Permission boundaries and SCPs set maximum permissions
Review unused permissions with Access Analyzer and last-used data

concepts.name: Q: How do you design a VPC? What is the difference between public and private subnets?
concepts.explanation: A VPC is a logically isolated network defined by a CIDR block and split into subnets across multiple availability zones. A public subnet has a route to an internet gateway and hosts resources that need direct inbound access, such as load balancers. A private subnet has no direct inbound internet route and uses a NAT gateway for outbound access; application servers and databases belong there. Security groups and NACLs control traffic, and VPC endpoints give private access to AWS services without crossing the internet.
keyPoints: Use non-overlapping CIDRs to allow peering, Transit Gateway or VPN
One NAT gateway per AZ for resilience, or one shared to save cost
Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB avoid NAT charges
Flow Logs help with network troubleshooting and auditing

concepts.name: Q: How do you make an application highly available and fault tolerant on AWS?
concepts.explanation: Spread instances across at least two availability zones behind an Application Load Balancer with health checks, run them in an Auto Scaling Group that replaces failed instances, and use managed multi-AZ data stores such as RDS Multi-AZ or Aurora, with replicated or versioned S3 storage. Keep servers stateless, store sessions in a cache, use Route 53 health checks and failover for regional resilience, and back up data with tested restores. Remove single points of failure and design for graceful degradation.
keyPoints: High availability protects against component or AZ failure; disaster recovery covers a regional loss
Define RPO and RTO and pick backup, pilot light, warm standby or active-active accordingly
Test failover with game days and chaos experiments
Autoscaling policies should react to load and health

concepts.name: Q: S3 storage classes, versioning, and how do you secure a bucket?
concepts.explanation: S3 offers storage classes from Standard for frequent access to Standard-IA, One Zone-IA, Intelligent-Tiering and the Glacier tiers for archives, with lifecycle rules moving or expiring objects automatically. Versioning keeps old versions to protect against overwrites and deletes. To secure a bucket I enable Block Public Access, use bucket policies and IAM with least privilege, encrypt with SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS, enforce TLS, enable access logging and Object Lock for compliance, and use VPC endpoints for private access.
keyPoints: Pre-signed URLs grant temporary access to private objects
Replication (CRR/SRR) supports DR and compliance
Never make a bucket public unless it is a deliberate static site behind CloudFront
S3 is strongly consistent for reads after writes

concepts.name: Q: EC2 vs Lambda vs ECS/Fargate vs EKS: when do you choose which?
concepts.explanation: EC2 gives full control of virtual machines and suits legacy apps, special hardware or steady workloads. Lambda runs short event-driven functions with no servers to manage and scales to zero, ideal for spiky or glue workloads but limited by execution time and cold starts. ECS with Fargate runs containers without managing servers, a simple way to run services on AWS. EKS provides managed Kubernetes for portability, ecosystem and large multi-team platforms at the cost of operational complexity.
keyPoints: Start with the simplest option that satisfies requirements
Cost depends on utilisation: steady load is often cheaper on instances or savings plans
Containers keep options open between all of them
Consider team skills and on-call burden

concepts.name: Q: How do you reduce AWS costs?
concepts.explanation: I begin with visibility using cost allocation tags, budgets, anomaly detection and Cost Explorer. Then I remove waste: idle or stopped instances, unattached volumes, old snapshots, unused load balancers and IPs. I right-size instances and databases, move to Graviton where compatible, use Savings Plans or Reserved Instances for steady workloads and Spot for fault-tolerant jobs, schedule non-production environments off outside working hours, add S3 lifecycle policies, and reduce data transfer with VPC endpoints and CDNs.
keyPoints: NAT gateway and cross-AZ data transfer are common hidden costs
Review costs per team monthly (FinOps)
Estimate Terraform changes with Infracost in pull requests
Autoscaling and serverless reduce paying for idle capacity

concepts.name: Q: What is the difference between an ALB, NLB and Classic LB, and how do health checks work?
concepts.explanation: An Application Load Balancer works at layer 7, routing by host, path, headers and supporting WebSockets, gRPC and authentication integrations. A Network Load Balancer works at layer 4 for TCP/UDP with very high throughput, low latency and static IPs. Classic Load Balancer is the legacy option. Load balancers send periodic health check requests to each target and stop routing traffic to targets that fail a configured number of checks, resuming when they pass again.
keyPoints: Health check endpoints should be fast and reflect readiness, not deep dependency status
Connection draining (deregistration delay) lets in-flight requests complete
A 502 from an ALB usually means a bad response from a target; 504 means timeout
Use path-based routing to share one ALB across services

concepts.name: Q: How do you securely give a CI/CD pipeline access to AWS?
concepts.explanation: I avoid static access keys. The pipeline authenticates with OpenID Connect: GitHub Actions or GitLab requests a short-lived token and assumes an IAM role whose trust policy restricts exactly which repository, branch or environment may assume it. The role has least-privilege permissions for just the deployment actions, and sessions expire automatically. Secrets that are still needed are stored in the CI secret store or AWS Secrets Manager.
keyPoints: Add conditions on sub and aud claims in the IAM trust policy
Use separate roles per environment with approvals for production
Audit with CloudTrail
Same pattern works for GCP Workload Identity Federation and Azure federated credentials

concepts.name: Q: A production RDS database is slow or running out of connections. What do you do?
concepts.explanation: I check CloudWatch and Performance Insights for CPU, IOPS, memory, connections and top SQL, and the slow query log. Typical fixes are adding missing indexes, fixing N+1 or heavy queries, adding connection pooling (RDS Proxy or PgBouncer), caching hot reads, adding read replicas for read traffic, and scaling the instance or storage. I also review recent deployments and schema changes, and make sure application pool sizes multiplied by instance counts do not exceed the database's maximum connections.
keyPoints: Take a snapshot before risky changes
Multi-AZ gives failover, not performance
Look for long-running transactions and locks
Alert on connections, replica lag, free storage and CPU credit balance

concepts.name: Q: What is the difference between monitoring and observability?
concepts.explanation: Monitoring checks known failure modes using predefined metrics, dashboards and alerts, answering "is the system healthy?". Observability is the ability to understand internal state from the telemetry a system emits — metrics, logs and traces — so you can investigate unknown problems and ask new questions without shipping new code. Monitoring is something you do; observability is a property of the system.
keyPoints: Three pillars: metrics (what and how much), logs (what happened), traces (where time went)
Correlate with trace IDs in logs and exemplars in metrics
OpenTelemetry standardises instrumentation
Good observability reduces mean time to detect and resolve

concepts.name: Q: What are SLI, SLO, SLA and error budget?
concepts.explanation: An SLI is a measurable indicator of service quality, such as the percentage of requests that succeed within 300 ms. An SLO is the internal target for that SLI, for example 99.9% over 30 days. An SLA is the external contract with penalties, usually looser than the SLO. The error budget is 100% minus the SLO — the amount of unreliability allowed — and it guides decisions: while budget remains the team ships features, and when it is exhausted they prioritise reliability work.
keyPoints: 99.9% allows about 43 minutes of downtime per 30 days
Alert on burn rate rather than raw thresholds
Choose SLIs from the user's perspective (availability, latency, correctness)
100% is the wrong goal; each extra nine costs far more

concepts.name: Q: What are the four golden signals?
concepts.explanation: Latency (how long requests take, separating successes from errors), traffic (demand such as requests per second), errors (rate of failed requests, including wrong results and timeouts) and saturation (how full the system is, such as CPU, memory, disk, queue depth or connection pools). Monitoring these four for every service covers most user-visible health problems.
keyPoints: RED method for services: rate, errors, duration
USE method for resources: utilisation, saturation, errors
Use percentiles (p95, p99) rather than averages for latency
Saturation often warns before users feel pain

concepts.name: Q: How does Prometheus work, and what are its metric types?
concepts.explanation: Prometheus pulls metrics over HTTP from the /metrics endpoint of targets at a configured interval, discovered statically or through service discovery such as Kubernetes. It stores samples in a local time-series database and is queried using PromQL; alerting rules are evaluated and sent to Alertmanager. Metric types are counter (monotonically increasing, use rate()), gauge (value up and down), histogram (bucketed observations for percentiles) and summary (client-side quantiles).
keyPoints: Pull model makes targets simple and health obvious (up metric)
Pushgateway is only for short-lived batch jobs
Long-term storage and horizontal scale need Thanos, Mimir or VictoriaMetrics
Beware high-cardinality labels; they explode memory use

concepts.name: Q: How do you design good alerts and avoid alert fatigue?
concepts.explanation: Alerts should be urgent, actionable and symptom-based: page a human only when users are affected or an SLO is burning fast, and send everything else to tickets or dashboards. Each alert needs a clear summary, severity, and a runbook link, use a for-duration to avoid flapping, and be routed and grouped by Alertmanager. I review noisy alerts regularly, delete the useless ones, and track pages per on-call shift as a health metric.
keyPoints: Multi-window burn-rate alerts on SLOs reduce noise
Cause-based alerts (high CPU) belong on dashboards unless they predict an outage
Test alerts and escalation paths before you need them
On-call load directly affects retention and quality

concepts.name: Q: Walk me through how you handle a production incident.
concepts.explanation: First I acknowledge the alert, assess severity and impact, and open an incident channel with defined roles such as incident commander, communications and operations. I focus on mitigation before root cause — rollback the last change, disable a feature flag, scale or fail over — and communicate status on a regular cadence. Once service is restored I confirm with metrics, keep monitoring, and within days run a blameless postmortem with a timeline, causes and tracked action items to prevent recurrence and improve detection.
keyPoints: Ask "what changed?" first: deploys, config, traffic, dependencies, certificates
Record a timeline as you go
Avoid multi-person debugging chaos: one person drives, others investigate in parallel lanes
Track MTTD and MTTR to prove improvement

concepts.name: Q: What is DevSecOps and how do you integrate security into pipelines?
concepts.explanation: DevSecOps embeds security throughout the delivery lifecycle instead of treating it as a final gate. In pipelines I add secret scanning and pre-commit hooks, SAST and dependency scanning on pull requests, container and IaC scanning, SBOM generation, image signing and verification, policy enforcement at deployment with admission controllers, and DAST plus runtime detection in later stages. Findings are triaged by severity with automated dependency update PRs, and security is shared with developers through clear feedback and guardrails.
keyPoints: Fail builds only on actionable high-severity issues to maintain trust
Short-lived credentials and least privilege protect the pipeline itself
Threat model new designs early
Tools: Trivy, Snyk, Semgrep, SonarQube, Checkov, gitleaks, cosign, Falco

concepts.name: Q: How do you secure a Kubernetes cluster?
concepts.explanation: Layered controls: restrict API access with RBAC and private endpoints, enable audit logging and secrets encryption, apply Pod Security Admission with the restricted profile and hardened securityContexts (non-root, read-only filesystem, dropped capabilities), use NetworkPolicies with default-deny, scan and sign images and admit only trusted ones, manage secrets externally, keep nodes and Kubernetes patched, and use runtime threat detection such as Falco. Cloud IAM integration (workload identity) removes static credentials.
keyPoints: Benchmarks: CIS Kubernetes, kube-bench, kubescape
Policy engines: Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
Avoid privileged containers and hostPath mounts
Separate environments and sensitive workloads by cluster or node pool

concepts.name: Q: How would you handle a leaked credential or secret in a Git repository?
concepts.explanation: Treat it as compromised immediately: revoke or rotate the credential first, then check access logs for misuse. After that remove it from history with git filter-repo or BFG, force-push and have collaborators re-clone, because deleting it in a new commit does not remove it from history or forks. Then prevent recurrence with pre-commit secret scanning, CI scanning, push protection, and moving secrets to a manager with short-lived credentials.
keyPoints: Rotating is mandatory; history rewriting is only cleanup
GitHub secret scanning and push protection catch common token formats
Audit what the credential could access and review CloudTrail or equivalent
Write a short postmortem and fix the process that allowed it

concepts.name: Q: What is a service mesh and when would you use one?
concepts.explanation: A service mesh adds a dedicated infrastructure layer for service-to-service communication, typically through sidecar proxies or node-level proxies controlled by a control plane such as Istio, Linkerd or Cilium. It provides mutual TLS, traffic management (retries, timeouts, canary splitting), observability and policy without changing application code. It is worth the added complexity and resource cost only with many services that need uniform security, traffic control and telemetry; smaller systems should use simpler tools first.
keyPoints: Sidecarless and ambient modes reduce overhead
Gateway API weights and libraries can cover simple canary needs
Misconfigured meshes are a common source of hard-to-debug latency
Evaluate the operational burden before adopting

concepts.name: Q: What are backup and disaster recovery best practices, and what are RPO and RTO?
concepts.explanation: RPO (recovery point objective) is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time, and RTO (recovery time objective) is the maximum acceptable downtime. Best practices are the 3-2-1 backup rule, immutable and encrypted backups in a separate account or region, automated schedules with retention, point-in-time recovery for databases, and — most importantly — regular restore tests and DR drills. Strategy options range from backup and restore to pilot light, warm standby and active-active as RPO and RTO tighten and cost rises.
keyPoints: Replication is not a backup; it copies mistakes and corruption
Document runbooks and measure the real RTO during drills
Back up configuration too: Terraform state, Kubernetes manifests, DNS and secrets
Protect backups from deletion with separate credentials and object lock

concepts.name: Scenario: Production site returns 502 errors after a deployment. What do you do?
concepts.explanation: I would confirm scope and timing, then check whether the errors started with the deployment. Since a 502 means the proxy or load balancer got a bad response from the backend, I check target health, whether the new Pods or instances are running and ready, and their logs for crashes, startup failures, wrong ports or missing configuration. If the new version is clearly at fault I roll back immediately to restore service, then reproduce in staging, fix the issue, and add a readiness check, smoke test or canary stage so the pipeline would catch it.
concepts.code:
kubectl rollout status deploy/api; kubectl get pods -l app=api
kubectl logs deploy/api --tail=100; kubectl describe pod <pod>
kubectl get endpoints api                   # any ready addresses?
kubectl rollout undo deploy/api             # mitigation
# non-K8s: systemctl status app; journalctl -u app -n 100; nginx error.log; ALB target health
keyPoints: State the order: scope, mitigate, diagnose, fix, prevent
Common causes: bad config or secret, wrong port, failing readiness, missing migration, dependency down
Compare image tag and digest actually running
Close with the preventive improvement

concepts.name: Scenario: A Kubernetes Pod keeps getting OOMKilled. How do you resolve it?
concepts.explanation: OOMKilled means the container exceeded its memory limit. I confirm with kubectl describe pod (last state, reason OOMKilled, exit code 137), look at memory usage over time in Grafana to see whether it is a steady leak, a spike at certain operations, or simply an under-sized limit. For JVM apps I check heap settings relative to the container limit. The fix is either to raise the limit and request with data to support it, tune the application (heap size, caching, batch size), or fix the leak using heap or profiler analysis, then add alerts on memory saturation.
concepts.code:
kubectl describe pod api-xyz | grep -A5 "Last State"
kubectl top pod api-xyz --containers
kubectl get pod api-xyz -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated}'
# Java: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75   (heap relative to the container limit)
# Prometheus: container_memory_working_set_bytes / kube_pod_container_resource_limits{resource="memory"}
keyPoints: Do not just keep increasing limits; find the trend
Memory request equal to limit gives predictable scheduling
VPA recommendations help right-size
Node-level memory pressure causes evictions, which look different from OOMKilled

concepts.name: Scenario: Design a CI/CD pipeline and deployment strategy for a new web application.
concepts.explanation: I would clarify requirements first: team size, release frequency, compliance and platform. Then propose trunk-based development with protected main, a PR pipeline running lint, tests, security scans and a container build, and a main pipeline that pushes an immutable SHA-tagged image, deploys to dev automatically, runs smoke and integration tests, promotes through staging, and deploys to production with a canary or rolling update gated by health metrics and automatic rollback. Infrastructure comes from Terraform, deployment via GitOps, secrets from a secret manager, and observability with dashboards, alerts and deployment markers.
concepts.code:
# PR:      lint -> unit tests -> SAST/SCA -> docker build (no push) -> trivy
# main:    build + push :sha -> sign -> update config repo -> ArgoCD deploys dev
# promote: smoke/integration -> staging -> e2e/perf -> approval -> prod (canary 10% -> 50% -> 100%)
# guard:   SLO/error-rate analysis aborts + rolls back automatically
keyPoints: Say how you handle database migrations, secrets and rollbacks explicitly
Mention metrics to track: DORA and pipeline duration
Offer a simpler alternative for a small team (single environment, rolling deploys)
Explain trade-offs, not only the ideal design

concepts.name: Scenario: How would you migrate a monolith on VMs to Kubernetes with minimal risk?
concepts.explanation: I would avoid a big-bang rewrite. First containerise the monolith as-is with a proper Dockerfile, externalise configuration and state, add health endpoints, logging to stdout and metrics. Stand up a platform with infrastructure as code, CI/CD and observability, run the container in staging, then shift production traffic gradually using weighted DNS or load balancer routing (canary) while keeping the old VMs as a rollback path.
