After stability is proven, extract services incrementally using the strangler fig pattern where it adds value.
keyPoints: Move state (sessions, uploads) out of the instance first
Keep data migration separate and reversible
Load test and rehearse rollback before cutover
Do not adopt Kubernetes if the team cannot operate it; ECS or Cloud Run may be enough

concepts.name: Scenario: Disk is 100% full on a production server. What do you do?
concepts.explanation: I find what is using space, free enough to restore service safely, then fix the cause. df -h shows the full filesystem and df -i checks inodes; du -xh --max-depth=1 or ncdu drills into directories. Usual culprits are logs, Docker images and volumes, temp files and core dumps. Safe quick wins are compressing or deleting old rotated logs, docker system prune for unused images, and clearing package caches. If space seems used with no files, lsof +L1 finds deleted-but-open files and restarting that process frees them. Afterwards I add log rotation, retention, and an 80% disk alert.
concepts.code:
df -h; df -i
sudo du -xh / --max-depth=2 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -20
sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=500M
docker system df && docker system prune -f
sudo lsof +L1 | head
keyPoints: Never delete application data or database files without certainty
Truncate an open log with : > file rather than rm
Add monitoring on usage growth trend, not just the threshold
On cloud volumes, extend the volume and filesystem as a stopgap

concepts.name: Scenario: Your application is slow only during peak hours. How do you investigate?
concepts.explanation: I start from the metrics: compare latency, traffic, error rate and saturation for the affected hours, and use traces to find which dependency or span has grown. Typical findings are database connection pool exhaustion, slow queries and missing indexes, CPU or memory saturation, insufficient autoscaling or slow scale-up, cache misses, external API slowness or noisy neighbours. I then reproduce with a load test, apply the targeted fix such as indexing, caching, pool tuning or scaling policies, and set SLO-based alerts and capacity planning for next time.
keyPoints: Look at percentiles (p95/p99), not averages
Check autoscaler lag: pods and nodes may take minutes to appear
Queue depth and thread pool saturation are classic hidden bottlenecks
Validate fixes with the same load test

concepts.name: Scenario: How do you achieve a zero-downtime deployment for an app with a database schema change?
concepts.explanation: Use the expand and contract pattern combined with a rolling or blue/green release. In the expand phase apply a backward-compatible migration, such as adding a nullable column, and deploy application code that works with both old and new schemas, writing to both if needed. Backfill data in batches, then switch reads to the new structure in a later release, and only after that stable period remove the old column in a contract migration. Each step can be rolled back independently.
keyPoints: Never combine an incompatible schema change with the code that needs it in one deploy
Run migrations as a separate controlled step, not on every replica start
Feature flags help switch behaviour safely
Take backups and rehearse on production-like data

concepts.name: Scenario: Design a highly available, scalable architecture for a web app on the cloud.
concepts.explanation: Place a CDN and WAF in front, route DNS to a load balancer spanning multiple availability zones, and run stateless application instances or containers in an autoscaling group or Kubernetes node groups in private subnets. Use a managed multi-AZ database with read replicas and a cache for hot data, object storage for files, queues for asynchronous work, and secrets and encryption through managed services. Add infrastructure as code, CI/CD, centralised logs, metrics and traces with SLO-based alerts, tested backups and a documented DR strategy sized by RPO and RTO. Finally discuss cost and the main failure modes.
concepts.code:
# Users -> CDN/WAF -> ALB (multi-AZ)
#            -> app tier (ASG / EKS, private subnets, autoscaling, stateless)
#            -> cache (Redis) + DB (Multi-AZ primary + read replica) + object storage
#            -> queue + workers for async jobs
# Cross-cutting: IaC, CI/CD, observability, secrets, backups, IAM least privilege
keyPoints: Ask about traffic, data size, consistency needs and budget before designing
Name single points of failure and how each is removed
Show scaling bottlenecks: database writes, shared state, third-party dependencies
Close with what you would build first versus later

concepts.name: Scenario: Your CI pipeline has become slow and flaky. How do you fix it?
concepts.explanation: I would measure first: capture duration per stage, failure rate and which tests fail intermittently. Then speed up using parallel jobs, dependency and Docker layer caching, path filters, test sharding, smaller base images, and faster runners. For flakiness I quarantine and track flaky tests with owners, remove shared state and time dependence, use ephemeral clean environments, pin dependencies, and add retries only for external transient failures. I report pipeline duration and success rate as team metrics so improvements stick.
keyPoints: Flaky tests destroy trust faster than slow ones
Move slow end-to-end checks to post-merge or nightly pipelines, keeping PR feedback fast
Use Testcontainers instead of shared databases
Treat the pipeline as a product with an owner

concepts.name: Scenario: A teammate accidentally deleted a production resource. How do you respond and prevent it?
concepts.explanation: First restore service: recover from backups, snapshots, versioned storage or by re-applying infrastructure as code, and communicate status. Do not blame the person; run a blameless review of how the system allowed it. Preventive measures include least-privilege access and no standing admin rights, MFA and just-in-time elevation, deletion protection and prevent_destroy on critical resources, versioning and object lock, change review through IaC pull requests with plan output, separate accounts for environments, audit logging, and regular restore tests.
keyPoints: Check CloudTrail or audit logs to understand exactly what happened
Terraform lifecycle prevent_destroy and RDS deletion protection are cheap safeguards
Use break-glass access with alerts for emergencies
Practise recovery so it is routine, not heroic

sections.title: Interview Q&A: Live Coding & Hands-On Tasks

concepts.name: Task: Write a production-ready Dockerfile for a Node.js app
concepts.explanation: Interviewers want to see multi-stage builds, layer caching by copying lockfiles first, a non-root user, a pinned base version, only production dependencies, and a health check. Explain each decision aloud as you write it.
concepts.code:
# Dockerfile
FROM node:24-alpine AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

FROM node:24-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:24-alpine AS runtime
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps  /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY package.json .
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
keyPoints: Copying package files before source keeps the npm ci layer cached
Add a .dockerignore for node_modules, .git and .env
Pin versions (and a digest for critical images) and rebuild regularly for patches
Mention scanning with Trivy and signing as extra credit

concepts.name: Task: Write a GitHub Actions workflow that tests, builds and pushes a Docker image
concepts.explanation: A strong answer triggers on pull requests and main, runs tests first, builds the image with caching, pushes only from main, uses the commit SHA as the tag, and uses GITHUB_TOKEN with minimal permissions rather than stored passwords.
concepts.code:
name: ci
on:
  pull_request:
  push: { branches: [main] }
permissions: { contents: read, packages: write }
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with: { node-version: 24, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci && npm test
  image:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v4
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
        with: { registry: ghcr.io, username: "${{ github.actor }}", password: "${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}" }
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          push: ${{ github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' }}
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max
keyPoints: needs: test makes the image job wait for tests to pass
Push only on main, build-only on pull requests
Mention adding a vulnerability scan before the push
Pin actions to commit SHAs in sensitive repositories

concepts.name: Task: Write a Kubernetes Deployment and Service with probes, resources and a safe rollout
concepts.explanation: Show requests and limits, readiness and liveness probes, a RollingUpdate strategy with maxUnavailable 0, labels matching the Service selector, and non-root security settings.
keyPoints: The Service selector must match the Pod template labels
Memory request equals limit for predictable behaviour
Add an HPA and a PodDisruptionBudget to complete the answer
Use an immutable image tag, never latest

concepts.name: Task: Write a Terraform configuration for an S3 bucket with remote state
concepts.explanation: Show provider and version constraints, a remote backend with locking, a bucket with encryption, versioning and public access blocked, variables and outputs, and tags.
keyPoints: Modern AWS provider splits bucket features into separate resources
The backend bucket itself is created separately (bootstrap) before use
Explain plan, apply, and why remote state with locking matters
Mention scanning with Checkov or Trivy before applying

concepts.name: Task: Write a Bash script that checks service health and retries
concepts.explanation: Demonstrate strict mode, functions, retries with backoff, clear exit codes and logging. Keep it short and explain how it would be used in a pipeline or cron.
concepts.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -Eeuo pipefail
URL="${1:?usage: $0 <url> [retries]}"
RETRIES="${2:-5}"

log() { printf '%s %s\n' "$(date +%FT%T)" "$*" >&2; }

for ((i = 1; i <= RETRIES; i++)); do
  code="$(curl -s -o /dev/null -m 5 -w '%{http_code}' "$URL" || true)"
  if [[ "$code" == "200" ]]; then
    log "healthy ($URL) on attempt $i"
    exit 0
  fi
  log "attempt $i/$RETRIES failed (status: ${code:-none})"
  sleep $((i * 2))                       # linear backoff
done
log "UNHEALTHY: $URL"
exit 1
keyPoints: Exit non-zero on failure so CI, cron or monitoring can react
Use curl timeouts (-m) so the script cannot hang
Run shellcheck and mention testing with bats if asked
For frequent checks prefer real monitoring (blackbox exporter) over cron scripts

concepts.name: Task: Write a Prometheus alert rule and a quick PromQL for error rate
concepts.explanation: Show an alert on the ratio of 5xx responses over a window, with a for duration, severity label and annotations including a runbook.
concepts.code:
groups:
  - name: api-slo
    rules:
      - alert: ApiHighErrorRate
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
            / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[5m])) > 0.02
        for: 10m
        labels: { severity: page }
        annotations:
          summary: "API 5xx ratio above 2% for 10 minutes"
          runbook_url: https://wiki.example.com/runbooks/api-5xx
keyPoints: rate() over a counter gives per-second increase; always use it on counters
Use for: to avoid flapping on brief spikes
A ratio is better than a raw count because it scales with traffic
Mention SLO burn-rate alerts for a stronger answer

concepts.name: Rapid Fire: Core Concept Differences
concepts.explanation: Short, precise contrasts are a favourite interview format. Memorise these one-line answers so you can respond instantly and then expand if asked.
concepts.code:
# Container vs VM                 shares host kernel, isolates processes | full guest OS on a hypervisor
# Image vs Container              read-only template | running instance + writable layer
# CMD vs ENTRYPOINT               default args (overridable) | the fixed executable
# COPY vs ADD                     plain copy | also extracts tar and fetches URLs (prefer COPY)
# ARG vs ENV                      build-time only | persists into the running container
# Volume vs Bind mount            Docker-managed storage | specific host path
# Docker vs Podman                daemon-based | daemonless, rootless-friendly, same CLI style
# Pod vs Container                one or more containers sharing network+storage | single process
# Deployment vs StatefulSet       stateless replicas | stable identity + storage per replica
# Deployment vs DaemonSet         N replicas anywhere | one per node
# Service vs Ingress              L4 stable endpoint | L7 HTTP routing (needs a controller)
# ClusterIP vs NodePort vs LB     internal | port on every node | cloud load balancer
# ConfigMap vs Secret             plain config | sensitive data (base64, not encryption)
# Liveness vs Readiness           restart if failing | remove from traffic if failing
# Requests vs Limits              reserved for scheduling | hard ceiling at runtime
# HPA vs VPA vs Cluster Autoscaler  more Pods | bigger Pods | more nodes
# Helm vs Kustomize               templates + packaging | patches on plain YAML
# Role vs ClusterRole             namespaced permissions | cluster-wide permissions
keyPoints: State the difference in one sentence, then give one example
Interviewers use these as warm-ups; clean fast answers build confidence
Link each pair to a real situation you have faced
If unsure, say what you do know and reason aloud

concepts.name: Rapid Fire: Tools & Practices Differences
concepts.explanation: A second set of quick contrasts covering CI/CD, infrastructure, cloud and operations terminology.
concepts.code:
# CI vs CD (delivery) vs CD (deployment)   integrate+test | always releasable, manual release | automatic release
# Blue/green vs Canary vs Rolling          full parallel env, flip | small % first | gradual replacement
# Terraform vs Ansible                     provision infra (declarative, state) | configure servers (agentless, YAML)
# Terraform vs CloudFormation              multi-cloud, HCL, state file | AWS-only, JSON/YAML, state managed by AWS
# Mutable vs Immutable infra               patch in place | replace with a new image
# Declarative vs Imperative                desired end state | explicit ordered steps
# Push vs Pull deployment (GitOps)         CI holds cluster creds | agent in cluster pulls from Git
# Merge vs Rebase                          preserves history, merge commit | linear history, rewrites commits
# Revert vs Reset                          new undo commit (safe, shared) | moves branch pointer (local)
# Fork vs Clone vs Branch                  your server copy | local copy | line of development
# SAST vs DAST vs SCA                      scan source | attack running app | scan dependencies
# Metrics vs Logs vs Traces                numbers over time | event records | request path across services
# SLI vs SLO vs SLA                        measurement | internal target | contractual promise
# MTTD vs MTTA vs MTTR                     time to detect | acknowledge | recover
# RPO vs RTO                               max data loss | max downtime
# Backup vs Replication                    point-in-time recovery copy | live copy that also copies mistakes
# Horizontal vs Vertical scaling           add more instances | bigger instance
# L4 vs L7 load balancer                   TCP/UDP by IP+port | HTTP routing by host/path/headers
# Security group vs NACL                   stateful, instance-level, allow only | stateless, subnet-level, allow+deny
# Forward proxy vs Reverse proxy           acts for clients | acts for servers (nginx, ALB)
# Authentication vs Authorisation          who are you | what may you do
# IAM user vs role                         long-term credentials | temporary assumed credentials
# Cron vs systemd timer                    simple schedule | units, logging, catch-up of missed runs
# Hard link vs Symlink                     same inode | path pointer
# Process vs Thread                        isolated memory | shares process memory
keyPoints: Prefer precise contrasts over long definitions
Add "when I would pick each" to sound experienced
Many of these map to chapters earlier in this cheatsheet — use search to revise a topic quickly
Finish your preparation by explaining a few of these aloud to a friend or recording yourself
